docs.title: 4.3 Sustainable City Features — F6 Revision
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP4/Concepts/4.3 Sustainable City Features (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
This is the "solution" half of every CP4 essay, and it matches the 2027 Section B fieldwork module "Building a Sustainable City" (the module that replaced Climate Change). Expect data-response items where you must identify a feature from a figure and then evaluate it.

The formula for every feature: measure → mechanism → pillar → limit
"Green roofs reduce the urban heat island effect (measure) because vegetation absorbs less heat than concrete and provides evaporative cooling (mechanism), advancing environmental sustainability (pillar) — but they are expensive to maintain on old buildings (limit)."
One sentence, all four elements, three marks.
chunks.heading: 4.3 Sustainable City Features — F6 Revision

chunks.text:
- Energy efficiency — insulation and efficient systems cut electricity demand for cooling/heating → lower emissions and lower running cost → environmental and economic pillars.
- Water conservation — rainwater harvesting and reuse reduce demand on supply systems; matters most where supply is stressed.
- Natural lighting — daylighting reduces lighting electricity; design feature (orientation, atriums) rather than add-on technology.
- Green materials — recycled/recyclable content lowers embodied energy; closes the loop on construction waste.
- Certification — schemes such as BEAM Plus give a measurable standard, which turns "green" from a claim into evidence for an exam answer.
chunks.heading: 1. Green building

chunks.text:
- Public transit (MTR, buses, trams) — high-capacity modes cut cars-per-journey → less congestion and less emissions. Mechanism: mode shift, not just new vehicles.
- Cycling and walking — zero-emission short trips; needs safe, connected infrastructure or people revert to cars.
- Pedestrian zones — remove vehicles from a street → air/noise improvement plus commercial footfall (a social/economic gain).
- Electric vehicles — cut tailpipe emissions; be precise: benefit depends on how the electricity is generated, and they do not solve congestion or road space.
chunks.heading: 2. Sustainable transport

chunks.text:
- Reduce → reuse → recycle → recover → dispose, in that order of preference — the hierarchy itself is examinable.
- Recycling (three-colour bins) — diverts material from landfill but depends on public participation and market prices for recyclables.
- Composting — organic waste becomes soil condition; also cuts landfill methane.
- Incineration with energy recovery — shrinks volume and generates electricity, but produces emissions and ash, and needs steady feedstock.
- The structural point: a city with no spare land has to move up the hierarchy, because disposal has nowhere to go.
chunks.heading: 3. Waste management

chunks.text:
- Parks — recreation, mental health, and permeable surface for drainage.
- Urban forestry / tree planting — shade + evapotranspiration cools streets; absorbs CO₂ and filters pollutants.
- Vertical gardens and roof gardens — green the built-up core where ground land is unavailable; reduce roof temperatures and building energy use.
chunks.heading: 4. Green space

chunks.text:
The examiners keep finding that students narrow "sustainable city" down to green space alone. The 2021 DSE report is explicit: most candidates "explained only generally the provision of 'green space', but with an incomplete understanding of the term", and their "understanding of the social and economic aspects of a sustainable city was rather poor".

So a sustainable-city answer must reach beyond parks and trees to the features that carry the other two pillars:

| Feature group | The feature examiners expect you to name | Which pillar it carries |
|---|---|---|
| Green space | Parks and urban parks as the 'city lungs' — fresh air, outdoor recreation, reduced heat island effect, habitat retained inside the urban area | Environmental, with a social gain |
| Environmental infrastructure | Sewage treatment facilities — the 2021 report notes only a few candidates explained their role in environmental protection | Environmental |
| Transport | Rail-based public transport, underground pedestrian links, cycling paths and pedestrian corridors separated from vehicle traffic | Environmental and social |
| Urban renewal | Rehabilitation and retrofitting — better building safety, extended useful life, improved appearance and living environment, and no demolition waste | Economic, environmental and social |
chunks.heading: 5. What the examiner means by a sustainable city

chunks.text:
Two terminology traps the HKEAA briefings name repeatedly
- "Green belt" is not "green space". A green belt is land withheld from development; urban green space is space provided inside the built-up area. They are opposites. The 2022, 2024 and 2026 briefings all penalise candidates who confused them.
- The country park and the nature reserve are not urban green space. They sit outside the urban area. The 2021 report rules that citing them as examples of urban green space is inappropriate.

Answer structure for "Discuss measures to build a sustainable city"
Pick three features from different groups (one building, one transport, one waste/green) → for each: mechanism + a named HK example + one limitation → close by judging which feature gives the largest gain for a land-scarce city.
chunks.heading: 5. What the examiner means by a sustainable city

chunks.text:
Common marks lost
- Feature named, mechanism missing ("trees are good").
- No example — HK specifics (MTR, three-colour bins, I·PARK1, BEAM Plus) are cheap marks.
- Claiming EVs = zero pollution without the energy-generation caveat.
- Ignoring land scarcity: in Hong Kong, every measure competes for space — that trade-off is the evaluation.
- Repeating the same pillar three times instead of showing economic, environmental and social gains.
- Treating "sustainable city" as a synonym for "green space" — sewage treatment, transport and renewal features carry the other pillars.
- Citing the country park or nature reserve as urban green space; they are outside the urban area.
chunks.heading: 5. What the examiner means by a sustainable city

chunks.text:
1. Explain how a green roof cools a city — give the physical mechanism, not just the label.
2. Why does public transport reduce two different urban problems?
3. Using the waste hierarchy, explain why incineration is a step above landfill but below recycling.
4. Give one limitation of each: green building, electric buses, urban parks.
5. A city can fund one measure only. Which do you choose for a land-scarce city, and why?
6. Name a feature of a sustainable city that earns a mark without being green space, and say which pillar it carries.

docs.title: 4.4 Hong Kong Case Studies — F6 Revision
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP4/Concepts/4.4 Hong Kong Case Studies (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
Hong Kong is the examinable city for CP4 — the syllabus specifies urban problems and sustainability in Hong Kong. Examiners reward named, specific evidence (an actual project, an actual scheme), and penalise generic "the government should…" statements. Treat each item below as a quote-able case.
chunks.heading: 4.4 Hong Kong Case Studies — F6 Revision

chunks.text:
- The problem: ageing buildings in older districts (weak structure, no lift, poor ventilation) coexist with heritage value.
- Mechanism of the trade-off: demolition + higher-density redevelopment increases floor area and modernises housing, but irreversibly removes streetscapes and community networks.
- Both sides must appear: renovation/conservation keeps social continuity and embodied materials (environmental + social); redevelopment delivers capacity and safety (economic). The examinable judgement is which district, which building, and who decides — density gains in one place can push pressure onto another.
chunks.heading: 1. Urban renewal — the core conflict

chunks.text:
- MTR expansion — rail as the spine of the network: high capacity, electric, punctual; mechanism = mode shift from private cars and cross-harbour road traffic. Note the linked land-use point: MTR stations concentrate development (rail + property integration), which is itself a sustainability argument (transit-oriented development).
- Bus route restructuring — feeder and trunk reorganisation reduces duplicated routes and transfers; a network efficiency measure rather than a new technology.
- Electric buses — cut tailpipe emissions along the densest corridors, improving street-level air quality where exposure is highest. Caveat worth making: the gain depends on how electricity is generated.
chunks.heading: 2. Transport

chunks.text:
- Imported electricity from the Mainland — Hong Kong generates little of its own fuel supply; imports diversify sources and can lower cost and local emissions, but create dependency (a vulnerability in an evaluation answer).
- Renewable pilot schemes — solar on government buildings, schools and slopes. Be honest about limits: dense high-rise shading and land scarcity cap yield, so renewables currently contribute a small share. The examinable point is why a wealthy, land-scarce city still struggles with renewables.
chunks.heading: 3. Energy

chunks.text:
- Three-colour recycling bins — source separation raises recovery, but participation and market prices for recyclables determine success.
- Landfill extension — all three strategic landfills have been approaching capacity for years; extension buys time, costs money and faces NIMBY siting opposition.
- Incinerator (I·PARK1 / the WTE facility) — volume reduction plus energy recovery; trade-offs are emissions control costs, ash disposal, and public acceptance.
- The structural narrative examiners like: no land → disposal cannot expand → the city must move up the waste hierarchy (reduce/reuse/recycle).
chunks.heading: 4. Waste

chunks.text:
Locational-advantage questions are the most common 4- and 6-mark items in CP4, and they are marked in a fixed way: every advantage must be paired with the map evidence that proves it. The advantage alone earns nothing; the evidence alone earns nothing. The pairing is what earns the mark.

RAISE PLS is the eight-factor checklist that covers virtually every locational advantage:

| | Factor | The question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| R | Relief | Is the land gentle or steep? Is there coastal land that can be reclaimed to provide flat ground? |
| A | Accessibility | Are there enough transport facilities — railway, road, highway? |
| I | Industrial land use | Is there industrial land use that enhances employment — or threatens the project with pollution? |
| S | Scenery | Is the area in beautiful landscape, with a hillside view or a sea view? |
| E | Environment | Is there enough greenery and open space? |
| P | Public utilities | Are there enough public facilities — power lines, water pipes? |
| L | Labour | Is there enough labour, such as a public housing estate or middle-class residential area? |
| S | Space | Is there enough space for further development? |
chunks.heading: 5. RAISE PLS — the locational-advantage checklist

chunks.text:
| Locational advantage | Map evidence |
|---|---|
| Space for further development | Abundant space on the runway; adequate space for the berthing of cruises |
| Deep sea (relief) | Submarine contour lines show depth of 5–10 m; a runway of 2,800 m bordering the sea |
| Wide bay for navigation | Located in the spacious part of Victoria Harbour / Kowloon Bay |
| Convenient land transport (accessibility) | A named main road (Prince Edward Road, Tseung Kwan O Road), trunk road or railway connecting to other districts |

The evidence must be specific
"Good accessibility" is not evidence. "Served by the MTR station and Prince Edward Road" is. Use a grid square, a place name, a named road, or a contour value. The 2012 DSE mark scheme credited answers such as "cross-boundary linkage with Shenzhen — Kong Sham Western Highway / Shenzhen Bay Bridge" and "sewage treatment plant at grid reference 069855".
chunks.heading: The worked example: the cruise terminal at Kai Tak (2008 AL Q1)

chunks.text:
| Case | Use it for |
|---|---|
| Tai Po New Town | Self-containment: clear land use zoning; industrial and residential land separated (Tai Po Industrial Estate, Science Park); abundant open space (Waterfront Park, golf course); low-density housing at the outskirts (Hong Lok Yuen); private and public housing coexisting (Tai Po Centre, Tai Yuen Estate); the old market and declared monuments preserved (Tai Po Market, Tai Po Old Market); the mall and hotel; the transport interchange |
| Hung Shui Kiu New Development Area | Urban sprawl and land use conflict: proximity to Tin Shui Wai and Yuen Long; cross-boundary linkage with Shenzhen; vacant land and scattered container yards; Yeung Hau Temple and Tang Ancestral Hall; hills at grid squares 0685 and 0686 conserved as green area |
| Sheung Wan / Sai Ying Pun | Inner-city urban renewal; Wing Lee Street, PMQ and the Blue House as preservation and revitalisation cases |
| Lantau Island and the Tung Chung New Town Extension | Reclamation; land use planning in a new district — commercial land concentrated in the south/southeast near the highway and MTR, low-density residential in the north/northwest along the coast |
| Kowloon City | Urban renewal at site X and the proposed plan for area Y: new building blocks, improved air ventilation and quality, a basement car park, a pedestrian street and open space, and a community facility |
chunks.heading: Other quotable Hong Kong cases from the paper

chunks.text:
Answer structure for a HK case study question
1. Name the scheme/project precisely.
2. Explain the mechanism of benefit (what it changes, physically or behaviourally).
3. State which pillar(s) it advances.
4. Give one limitation specific to Hong Kong (land, density, cost, dependency, participation).
5. Verdict: effective to what extent — and under what condition.

Common marks lost
- Describing the scheme without saying why it helps (no mechanism).
- Inventing numbers — if you don't know a figure, argue from structure instead of guessing.
- Claiming success where the mechanism is weak (bins exist ≠ recycling happens; EVs ≠ clean grid).
- Ignoring land scarcity, the single most Hong Kong-specific constraint.
- Using an LDC example in a Hong Kong question.
- Giving the locational advantage with no map evidence, or the evidence with no advantage — the mark scheme is a two-column table and each pair is worth the mark.
- Vague evidence. "Good transport" scores nothing; "the West Rail station and Kong Sham Western Highway" scores.
chunks.heading: Other quotable Hong Kong cases from the paper

chunks.text:
1. Explain the urban-renewal trade-off using two of the three pillars.
2. How does MTR expansion reduce both congestion and air pollution?
3. Why is importing Mainland electricity both a gain and a risk?
4. Use the waste hierarchy to justify incineration in a land-scarce city, then give its strongest objection.
5. Name three Hong Kong waste measures and state, for each, what determines whether it actually works.
6. Write two RAISE PLS factors for the Kai Tak cruise terminal, each with the specific map evidence that would earn the mark.

chunks.heading: Quick self-check

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
This is the "who delivers it" section. Answers that name measures but never identify the actor (planner, government, community) lose the mechanism. The examinable distinction is regulation vs incentive vs participation — three different levers with different strengths.
chunks.heading: 4.5 Planning Strategies — F6 Revision

chunks.text:
- Zoning — assigns residential, commercial, industrial and other uses to land. Mechanism: it prevents incompatible mixing (industry next to homes) and anticipates problems rather than fixing them later. Limit: rigid zones can create long commutes when jobs and homes are separated — a genuine sustainability cost.
- Building control (height, density, setbacks) — sets how much can be built. Mechanism: density limits protect light/ventilation; controlled density near transit supports public-transport viability. Tension: high density makes efficient services but can worsen overcrowding.
- Green belts — land reserved from development. Mechanism: they permanently cap urban sprawl and protect recreational/ecological space. Limit: they raise land prices inside the boundary and can push development further out — say so; it is a top-band evaluation point.
chunks.heading: 1. Town planning — shaping land use

chunks.text:
| Lever | How it works | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| Regulation — emission standards, mandatory requirements | Sets a floor; non-compliance is penalised | Immediate, universal coverage | One-size-fits-all; can be gamed; no reward for exceeding the floor |
| Economic incentive — environmental taxes, charges, green-building subsidies | Changes the price, so behaviour changes voluntarily | Flexible, encourages innovation | Cost of administration; may be too weak to change behaviour |
| Provision/investment — building transit, bins, treatment works | Government supplies the alternative | Enables change that individuals cannot | Expensive; needs maintenance; dependent on budgets |

Use the table's logic in essays: regulation stops the worst behaviour, incentives encourage the best, provision makes either possible.
chunks.heading: 2. Government policies — three levers

chunks.text:
- Public consultation — residents' knowledge (noise, traffic, local use) improves decisions; mechanism = better information + perceived legitimacy, so schemes face less opposition.
- NGO participation — environmental groups monitor, campaign and run programmes that government does not have capacity for; they also hold decision-makers accountable.
- Education/awareness — changes individual behaviour (littering, recycling, energy use). Honest evaluation: education is slow and uncertain — it works only where alternatives exist. A person told to recycle with no nearby facility will not.
chunks.heading: 3. Community involvement — the social pillar in action

chunks.text: "Identify the urban renewal strategy" is a 1-mark question, so the answer is the strategy name and nothing else. Discrimination is by the defining feature:
chunks.heading: 4. The five urban-renewal strategies — and how to tell them apart

chunks.text:
| Strategy | Suitable for | Hong Kong example | Defining feature |
|---|---|---|---|
| Redevelopment | Very old buildings in poor condition or with structural danger; buildings with or without historical, cultural or architectural value | Kwun Tong Town Centre; Lei Tung Street, Wan Chai | Demolish and rebuild; greatly increases floor space; involves resettlement and high land-resumption cost |
| Preservation | Buildings with historical, cultural or architectural value | Wing Lee Street, Sheung Wan; Blue House, Wan Chai; PMQ | Keeps the building; no resettlement; preserves heritage and local character; does not increase floor space |
| Revitalisation | Using the special features of heritage sites to revive the community; turning heritage sites into new community hubs | PMQ, Sheung Wan; Tai Kwun, Central | Keeps the building but gives it new uses and new life — new activities, new jobs, tourism |
| Rehabilitation | Proper repair and maintenance of old buildings | General old buildings in the inner city | Slows urban decay by extending the life of the building; low cost and time-efficient; no demolition, no extra floor space |
| Retrofitting | Upgrading buildings to meet modern standards and enhance living quality | — | Upgrades facilities (appearance, hygiene, services) rather than repairing structure; no demolition, no extra floor space |
chunks.heading: 4. The five urban-renewal strategies — and how to tell them apart

chunks.text:
The one-line discriminator
Redevelopment demolishes and rebuilds (more floor space, resettlement, high cost). Preservation keeps the building exactly as it is. Revitalisation keeps the building but changes what happens inside it. Rehabilitation and retrofitting repair or upgrade in place — cheapest, no new floor space, no demolition waste.
chunks.heading: 4. The five urban-renewal strategies — and how to tell them apart

chunks.text: The exam asks candidates to compare land development methods. Each method has a gain and a cost under all three pillars, and each comes with a named example:
chunks.heading: 5. Ways of increasing Hong Kong's land supply

chunks.text:
| Method | Gain | Cost / conflict | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Building new towns and NDAs/PDAs | Land for commercial and other uses; owners can sell and profit; local jobs; a well-planned community with more open space; eases overcrowding by dispersing population | Higher farmland rents; higher infrastructure cost at remote sites; congestion on trunk roads; land resumption costly and slow; urban encroachment harms habitats; loss of traditional rural culture; green-group and villager opposition; longer, more expensive commutes | Nine new towns since the 1970s–90s; NDAs/PDAs in the north-east and north-west New Territories |
| Developing brownfield sites | Uses land more efficiently; releases land for uses; cheap to develop because infrastructure usually exists; eases rural land use conflict | Land resumption costly and slow; congestion if it becomes a large residential area; existing operations may not be relocatable, so businesses close and unemployment follows; opposition from owners and users, e.g. open storage operators | Former container yards in the New Territories |
| Reclamation | Large pieces of flat land; planning and development easier on new land; no land resumption needed | High reclamation and infrastructure cost; causes water pollution; damages wildlife habitats and marine life; loses natural coastal scenery; opposition from green groups, fishermen and the public | Victoria Harbour historically; the Protection of Harbour Ordinance now keeps new reclamation outside the harbour |
| Rock cavern development | Releases ground space; excavated rock can be used for construction and reclamation; placing unpopular facilities in caverns eases land use conflict | High construction and relocation cost; digging may disturb natural drainage and soil structure; no natural light or ventilation, so the environment is less desirable | The Sha Tin sewage treatment work moving to Ah Kung Kok, Tai Shui Hang |
| Reuse of ex-quarry sites | Releases land for housing, commercial and community facilities; cheap in the main urban area as infrastructure exists; improves a poor landscape | A large residential area increases traffic and crowding; a suburban site raises transport costs and commuting time | Anderson Road Quarry, Sau Mau Ping; Lamma Island |
| Underground space development | Frees above-ground space; underground pedestrian links relieve crowd and traffic congestion; reduces ground-level air pollution; land for community facilities | High construction cost; no natural light or ventilation; prolonged disruption to traffic, businesses and residents during construction | Victoria and Causeway Bay underground space development |
| Developing the Fanling golf course | 1.72 km² of complete or 0.32 km² of partial development; government-owned, so no land resumption needed; serves only about 2,200 members | High infrastructure cost; urban encroachment damages the countryside; around 30,000 trees, some old and valuable, may be removed; three historical buildings and around 150 ancestral graves and urns may face indigenous opposition; hosts international golf events, so development damages Hong Kong's image as an international city | The Fanling golf course |
| Converting industrial buildings | Makes good use of idle space; owners earn profit; eases land use conflict with nearby residential areas; can promote creative industries as art studios | Difficult and costly to renovate to the building codes for residential or commercial use | Fo Tan, Kowloon Bay, Kwun Tong |
| Redevelopment | Uses land resources more effectively; stimulates the property market; more floor space eases overcrowding and improves the living environment | High compensation cost and time for land resumption; higher rents close local shops; construction waste; loss of heritage and character; resettlement destroys social networks; heavier transport burden on low-income households resettled to suburbs; gentrification raises living costs | Kwun Tong; Lei Tung Street, Wan Chai |
chunks.heading: 5. Ways of increasing Hong Kong's land supply

chunks.text:
"Green belt" is not "green space"
A green belt is land withheld from development; urban green space is space provided inside the built-up area. The HKEAA briefings for 2022, 2024 and 2026 each penalise candidates who confuse the two. If a question asks you to develop green belts, you are arguing to remove a constraint on development — so the answer must address what the green belt was protecting.

Answer structure for "Evaluate planning strategies for a sustainable city"
1. Group measures by actor: planning (regulation) / government (incentive + provision) / community (participation).
2. For each: mechanism → named example → one strength and one limitation.
3. Show interaction: regulation without provision fails; provision without participation fails (bins without habits).
4. Conclude: which combination suits a land-scarce, high-density city, and why.
chunks.heading: 5. Ways of increasing Hong Kong's land supply

chunks.text:
Common marks lost
- Confusing a policy with its outcome ("the government bans pollution" ≠ cleaner air).
- Treating community involvement as free support — consultation costs time and can delay projects.
- Missing the green-belt counter-argument (higher prices / displaced development).
- No actor named: "something should be done" scores nothing.
- Forgetting Hong Kong's context — density and land scarcity change which lever works best.
- Confusing redevelopment with rehabilitation or revitalisation — identify the strategy by its defining feature, not by its name.
- Treating "green belt" and "green space" as the same thing; they are opposites.
- Comparing land development methods by listing only gains, with no cost under the economic, environmental and social pillars.
chunks.heading: 5. Ways of increasing Hong Kong's land supply

chunks.text:
1. Explain how zoning reduces an environmental problem before it occurs.
2. Distinguish an environmental tax from an emission standard — mechanism and trade-off.
3. Why does a recycling campaign fail if no collection system exists?
4. Give one way green belts help sustainability and one way they harm it.
5. Which lever would you use to make buildings more energy-efficient — regulation, incentive, or provision? Justify with a mechanism.
6. A photograph shows an old tenement with its façade repaired, services upgraded and the building still standing. Name the strategy, and name the strategy it is not, with the reason.

docs.title: 4.6 Challenges of Sustainable Development — F6 Revision
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP4/Concepts/4.6 Challenges of Sustainable Development (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
This part is the evaluation engine of CP4. Every "Discuss / Evaluate / To what extent" question is answered here: a measure is only sustainable if the conflict it creates is acceptable and the implementation is feasible. Students who reach for these arguments leave the top band; students who only praise measures do not.
chunks.heading: 4.6 Challenges of Sustainable Development — F6 Revision

chunks.text:
Development vs conservation
- Mechanism: land is finite — a site used for a park or preserved habitat is unavailable for housing or commerce, and vice versa. Every green-space decision in a land-scarce city has an opportunity cost.
- Signature case logic: urban renewal — rebuild (capacity, safety) or conserve (heritage, community, embodied materials).

Economic vs environmental (short-term vs long-term)
- Mechanism: environmental measures carry upfront cost and often delayed, diffuse benefits, while businesses and governments are rewarded on short horizons. Hence "we cannot afford it now" recurs — and is the argument sustainability is designed to answer (borrowing from the future generation).
- Example logic: green building standards raise construction cost but cut decades of running cost.

Individual vs collective
- Mechanism: sustainable outcomes are aggregate — one extra car, one unrecycled bag seems trivial alone, but multiplied by the population it defines the problem. Individuals bear private costs (effort, money) for collective gains → free-rider behaviour.
- Example logic: recycling participation; why incentives or regulation are often needed alongside education.
chunks.heading: 1. Conflicts — the three trade-offs

chunks.text:
- Cost — sustainable technology and retrofits are expensive; budgets compete with housing, health and transport. Public acceptance of charges/taxes is weak, so funding is politically fragile.
- Technology — solutions are not equally available: renewable generation is limited by land and weather in a dense city; some treatments need skills or infrastructure the city lacks. "Technically possible" ≠ "available here".
- Public acceptance / behavioural change — measures that change routines (separation of waste, fewer car trips, higher charges) meet habit and resistance; without compliance, the mechanism never fires. This is the single most common reason a well-designed scheme fails.
chunks.heading: 2. Implementation issues — why measures underdeliver

chunks.text: These are the specific obstacles Hong Kong's own renewal projects ran into. Each one is a mechanism you can attach to a real case.
chunks.heading: 3. Why implementation underdelivers — the six recurring obstacles

chunks.text:
| Obstacle | The mechanism, as it actually works |
|---|---|
| Land assembly | Inner-city land ownership is commonly complicated. Some owners have emigrated or died, so the government cannot even approach them; others are unsatisfied with the compensation and will not sell. The project cannot start until the site can be assembled. |
| Relocation and resettlement | Residents are reluctant to move because of close social networks and neighbourhood relationships. They cannot resettle in the original location because rents rise. After moving they live far from their workplace and face higher commuting costs, while businesses lose their customer network and cannot afford higher rents in the original or other districts. |
| Time | The government needs a long period to persuade owners and residents to accept compensation and resettlement. The Kwun Tong town centre project commenced in 2007 and land resumption was still not completed in 2016. |
| Financial | High burden from land resumption, compensation and resettlement of owners of domestic and non-domestic properties and tenants. The estimated cost of the Kwun Tong town centre was multi-billion dollars. |
| Conflicting stakeholder interests | Renewal projects may not gain the agreement of conservation groups and communities. Revitalisation and preservation may emphasise the external appearance of a building without reshaping its internal cultural and historical context; redevelopment may destroy buildings with historical, cultural or architectural value. |
| New environmental problems | Redevelopment creates construction waste, exerting further pressure on the landfills. Without comprehensive planning — particularly in projects carried out by private developers — the height and density of new commercial and residential buildings may be incompatible with the area. |
chunks.heading: 3. Why implementation underdelivers — the six recurring obstacles

chunks.text:
Link each obstacle to the right pillar
Land assembly, time and finance are economic and implementation obstacles. Resettlement is a social obstacle that also feeds back into the economy through commuting costs and lost customer networks. Conflicting stakeholder interests is the social pillar in difficulty form. New environmental problems are the environmental pillar in difficulty form.
A top-band answer names the obstacle, the mechanism, and the case it happened in.

Answer structure for the top-band evaluation
1. Acknowledge the measure's benefit (one sentence, with mechanism).
2. Name the specific conflict it creates (which two pillars clash).
3. State the implementation constraint (cost / technology / acceptance) in this city's context.
4. Resolve or weigh them: under what condition does the benefit survive the trade-off?
A closing sentence of this form is worth a mark on its own: "The measure is sustainable only if its upfront cost is met and public compliance is secured; otherwise it shifts rather than solves the problem."
chunks.heading: 3. Why implementation underdelivers — the six recurring obstacles

chunks.text:
Common marks lost
- Listing conflicts as abstract nouns with no mechanism ("there are trade-offs").
- No Hong Kong context — these arguments must be attached to a real case.
- Evaluating only cost, ignoring acceptance and technology (examiners award each distinct constraint).
- Treating conflict as failure: sustainability is managed conflict — say how it is managed.
- Contradicting yourself: praising a measure earlier, then denying all costs later.
- Writing the pros and cons of renewal strategies and stopping there. The 2020 DSE report noted "few candidates applied the concepts of sustainable city in their discussions" — the evaluation has to be run through the pillars, not left as a list.
- Failing to make a judgement. "Redesign of the old urban areas is an important measure" is not a verdict.
chunks.heading: 3. Why implementation underdelivers — the six recurring obstacles

chunks.text:
1. Explain the development-vs-conservation conflict using one Hong Kong site or project.
2. Why do environmental benefits arrive later than economic costs — and why does that matter for policy?
3. Use the free-rider idea to explain why education alone may not deliver recycling.
4. Give one cost, one technology limit and one acceptance problem facing a waste measure in Hong Kong.
5. Complete: "This measure is sustainable only if …" — then defend the sentence with two mechanisms.
6. Pick one of the six obstacles above and explain it as a chain: obstacle → mechanism → who carries the cost → pillar affected.

chunks.heading: 2.3 Infrastructure Problems

chunks.text:
- Physical symptoms: ageing/deteriorating buildings; poor structures; high fire risk; unauthorised building works; about 5,000 buildings aged 50+; high housing costs; lack of greening and public facilities; heat island effect; narrow streets, one-way traffic; mixed land use (factories/shops on lower floors); air, noise and visual pollution
- Social symptoms: declining population; economic restructuring (manufacturing and low-order commercial decline); fewer jobs, high unemployment; poverty, high crime; marginalisation of new immigrants and ethnic minorities
- Three causes of decay (mark these, not the symptoms): (1) early development to a lower building standard + outdated town planning; (2) suburbanisation hollowing out the inner city; (3) subdivided flats and in-migration of low-income residents
- Causal chain: urbanisation (natural increase) → suburbanisation (higher-income leave) → loss of attraction for new commercial activity + no maintenance of old buildings → urban decay
- Do not list gentrification as a cause — it is a consequence of renewal
chunks.heading: 2.4 Urban Decay — the inner-city half

chunks.text: Full expansion (definitions, causes, impacts, measures, HK specifics, DSE-2014 Q5 essay structure): 4.2 Urban Problems (F6 Revision) §5
chunks.heading: 2.5 Urban Encroachment, Urban Sprawl and Suburbanisation — the fringe half

chunks.text:
- Urban sprawl — horizontal expansion of urban land uses into rural areas, along main roads
- Suburbanisation — residents move to the suburbs
- Urban encroachment — rural land uses are fully changed to urban land uses
- Causes: inner-city push factors (poor living environment, overcrowding, pollution, expensive rent, congestion) + suburban pull factors (better environment, cheaper rent, quiet, transport, more space) + population growth + economic development + government planning + transport development (raises accessibility, lowers cost/time, enables longer commutes → longer-distance sprawl)
- Encroaching land uses: residential (new towns, low-density housing), transport (Western Corridor), industrial (Tai Po / Yuen Long / Tseung Kwan O estates), agricultural (farmland decline and abandonment)
- Positive impacts on the suburb: housing supply, better living environment and facilities, improved transport, rising land value, dispersed economic activity and jobs, greenbelts and pollution avoidance in new towns only
- Negative impacts: agricultural decline and rising land rent; abandoned land; farm labour shortage; land/water/air/noise pollution; flooding (sediment blocks rivers, more concrete runoff); habitat damage; rural decay, rural poverty, land-use conflict, land acquisition conflict, monument damage, lifestyle change
- Five measures: new-town development; environmental conservation (green belts, more greening); environmental impact assessment (limits and monitors rural land use); public participation; land-use zoning and regulation of farmland
chunks.heading: 2.5 Urban Encroachment, Urban Sprawl and Suburbanisation — the fringe half

chunks.text:
A. Land, farming and land-use conflict: farmland loss and agricultural decline (rents and production costs rise, farmland abandoned awaiting redevelopment, farm labour shortage as young people avoid primary production); abandoned land; land-use conflict as rural uses are displaced by temporary car-repairing workshops and container storage; rising rural land prices (speculators outbid farmers — the engine of abandonment).

B. Environment: land/water/air/noise pollution from construction, settlements and road networks; flooding by two mechanisms — sediment blocks rivers so bankfull discharge decreases, and more concrete raises surface runoff; ecosystems upset — vegetation cleared, wildlife habitats damaged, the pleasant rural environment destroyed.

C. Rural society and culture: rural decay (rural economy can no longer support social facilities → rural poverty → isolated villages fall into ruin); land acquisition → resident opposition and social conflict; damage to historical monuments; changes in lifestyle (Mapopo farm, Ma Shi Po); self-containment is the aim of a new town so it does not export commuting and congestion to the city.
chunks.heading: 2.5a The problems urban encroachment causes in the suburb (grouped)

chunks.text:
Book framing (Problems → Causes → Impacts), use the four-row structure: land/housing shortage (surging population, limited developable land) → housing shortage, congested living environment, urban sprawl; land-use conflict → incompatible land uses adjacent, damaging natural environment and threatening endangered species, hindering agriculture, lowering living standards; transport problems → heavy internal and external transport, noise and air pollution; solid waste → enormous municipal waste, declining landfill lifespan, incineration causing air pollution.

Two conflicts that drive CP4's second half: (1) urban development vs conservation of the natural environment — by urban encroachment; (2) urban development vs conservation of historical sites and cultural heritage — by urban encroachment AND inner-city redevelopment.
chunks.heading: 2.5a The problems urban encroachment causes in the suburb (grouped)

| 8 | Impact assessment | Both | S/ENV |

Planning instruments: Outline Zoning Plan (OZP) · Development Permission Area Plan (DPA Plan) · Development Scheme Plan (DSP).
Conservation designations: country parks · green belts · SSSI · Special Areas · Marine Parks · Marine Reserves · Hong Kong Global Geopark.

Public participation vs consultation: participation = forums and exhibitions, two-way, more direct, longer; consultation = opinion collection from identified groups and technical experts, one-way, less direct, shorter. Participation is the stronger tool.

EIA vs SIA: EIA assesses environmental impact before major projects, reduces negative impacts, studies alternatives and mitigation. SIA assesses the social needs of the affected community and minimises impacts on livelihoods.

chunks.heading: 6A.1 Examination tendency (pack page 2)

chunks.text:
Relief · Accessibility · Industrial land use · Scenery · Environment · Public utilities · Labour · Space.
Every advantage must be paired with the map evidence that proves it. The pack's worked example is the 2008 Kai Tak cruise terminal: space on the runway; submarine contours showing 5-10 m depth; a wide bay in Victoria Harbour / Kowloon Bay; named trunk roads or railways.
chunks.heading: 6A.2 The locational-advantage checklist: RAISE PLS (pack page 6)

chunks.text:
- Redevelopment — demolish and rebuild; greatly increases floor space; example Kwun Tong Town Centre.
- Preservation — keep the building; no resettlement; keeps local character; example Wing Lee Street, Sheung Wan.
- Revitalisation — keep the building, give it new uses and new life; example PMQ, Sheung Wan.
- Rehabilitation — proper repair and maintenance; slow urban decay; low cost; cannot increase floor space.
- Retrofitting — upgrade facilities to modern standards and enhance living quality.
chunks.heading: 6A.3 The five urban-renewal strategies (pack page 9)

chunks.text: Building new towns and NDAs/PDAs · Developing brownfield sites · Reclamation · Rock cavern development (Sha Tin sewage treatment work moving to Ah Kung Kok) · Reuse of ex-quarry sites (Anderson Road Quarry; Lamma) · Underground space development (Victoria and Causeway Bay) · Developing the Fanling golf course (1.72 km² complete / 0.32 km² partial; ~2,200 members; ~30,000 trees; ~150 ancestral graves) · Converting industrial buildings (Fo Tan, Kowloon Bay, Kwun Tong) · Redevelopment (Kwun Tong; Lei Tung Street, Wan Chai).
chunks.heading: 6A.5 Land supply methods (pack pages 10-15)

chunks.text:
- Describing urban decay instead of accounting for it (2020 DSE).
- Confusing "green belt" with "green space" — named in the 2021 report and again in the 2022, 2024 and 2026 HKEAA briefings.
- Citing the country park or nature reserve as urban green space — ruled out in the 2021 report.
- Stating gentrification as a cause of urban decay — it is a consequence of renewal (2020 report).
- Listing the merits of urban planning without referring to the setting (2021 report).
- Answering about urban problems but describing the site's locational characteristics instead (2021 report).
- Mixing up land use zoning and self-contained (2021 report).
- Listing only land-use types read off the map instead of analysing them (2021 report).
- Writing renewal strategies' pros and cons without applying the sustainable city concepts (2020 report).
- Answering locational advantage from a real-estate developer's perspective when the question asked about sustainable development (2021 report).

chunks.text:
1. Hot and dry summer → High evaporation

  • Strong sunlight and high temperature increase evaporation rate

  • Water evaporates from soil surface

2. Water table + Capillary action

  • Water table = top of groundwater

  • Capillary effect draws water upward through soil pores against gravity

3. Water rises, carrying salts

  • Water moves from water table to surface

  • Dissolved salts (e.g., NaCl) are carried upward with the water

4. Water evaporates, salts remain

  • Surface water evaporates

  • Salts are left behind in topsoil

5. Over-irrigation worsens the problem

  • Excess water raises the water table

  • More capillary action = more water movement

  • Irrigation water adds more salts

  • More evaporation = more salt accumulation

6. Result

  • White salty crust forms on surface

  • Soil becomes unsuitable for plant growth
chunks.heading: Soil Salinisation: Step-by-Step Explanation

chunks.text:
Predicted Grade Test P1.pdf
• Potential Evaporation (PE): Maximum evaporation possible if unlimited water available. Depends on temperature, humidity, wind, solar radiation.

• Actual Evaporation (AE): Actual water evaporated. Limited by water availability.

• Precipitation (P): Water input from rainfall.
  ───

Key Relationships

1. When P > Ep (Precipitation exceeds potential evaporation)

  • Soil moisture surplus

  • Ea = Ep (all potential evaporation is met)

  • Excess water → runoff or groundwater recharge

2. When P < Ep (Precipitation less than potential evaporation)

  • Soil moisture deficit

  • Ea = P (evaporation limited by water supply)

  • Soil dries out, moisture reserves depleted

3. Always true: Ea ≤ Ep

  • Ea cannot exceed Ep (can only evaporate what's available or what atmosphere can take)
chunks.heading: Relationship Between Hydrological Components

chunks.text:
|              | Saline Soil                                     | Salinisation                                                              |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Cause    | Natural climate conditions                      | Human activity (misuse of irrigation)                                     |
| Location | Southern California (arid climate)              | Irrigated agricultural areas worldwide                                    |
| Process  | Hot + dry → high evaporation → no rain to leach | Over-irrigation → water table rises → capillary action → salts accumulate |
| Example  | Imperial Valley's natural salt-affected soil    | Imperial Valley (Salton Sea area)                                         |

Key Difference:

  • Saline soil = Natural

  • Climate creates it (hot, dry, low rain)

  • "This land is naturally saline"

• Salinisation = Human-induced

  • Irrigation misuse creates it

  • "Poor irrigation practices caused salinisation"

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
The framework expects you to apply concepts accurately and consistently to contemporary issues. CP5 questions ask you to sort factors into the right system and then explain how each factor limits or raises output — a factor list alone earns little.
chunks.heading: 5.1 Agricultural Systems — F6 Revision

chunks.text:
The agricultural ecosystem (the farm as a natural system)
- Solar energy — the ultimate input: sunlight drives photosynthesis, so radiation, day length and cloudiness set the ceiling on yield.
- Water — rainfall or irrigation; both deficiency and surplus damage crops.
- Soil — nutrients, structure, drainage; soil fertility is what a season can draw on.
- Labour — the human work force available at planting/harvest peaks.
- Capital — money inputs: machinery, seeds, fertiliser.

The economic system (the farm as a business)
- Land — the space, and its rent/cost — an economic, not physical, constraint.
- Labour — as hired/paid work: wage cost and availability, not raw effort.
- Capital — as investment: machinery, loans, creditworthiness.
- Management — technology and skills: crop choice, timing, marketing.

The classic exam trap
Labour and capital appear in both systems — so naming them isn't enough. You must say which sense you mean: "labour as a physical input (enough hands at harvest)" vs "labour as a cost (wage rates)". The distinction is the mark.
chunks.heading: 1. Production factors — two systems, don't mix them

chunks.text:
Answer structure for "Explain factors affecting agricultural productivity"
1. Select the factors the question's system actually uses (physical vs economic).
2. For each: state it → give the mechanism ("high temperature increases the rate of photosynthesis, so …") → quantify or exemplify where possible.
3. Finish with the binding constraint: which single factor is limiting yield here — the factor that can't simply be added.
chunks.heading: 1. Production factors — two systems, don't mix them

chunks.text:
| | Subsistence | Commercial | Organic |
|---|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Feed the household | Sell for profit | Sell, using natural methods |
| Scale | Small, often fragmented | Large, mechanised | Varies (small → large) |
| Technology | Low, traditional | High, capital-intensive | Low synthetic inputs; skilled knowledge needed |
| Surplus / risk | Little surplus → high famine risk | Surplus + storage → buffer | Lower yields, higher price/premium market |

Why the spectrum matters in essays: movement from subsistence → commercial is exactly the process CP5 calls agricultural development, and it is the main long-run answer to famine. Organic sits on its own axis — it is about method, not scale: it can be practised on a smallholding or a corporate farm.

Mechanisms worth quoting: commercial farming raises output through machinery, irrigation, fertiliser and improved seed, and reduces volatility through storage and market access; subsistence farming's thin surplus means one bad season becomes hunger.

Answer structure for "Compare subsistence and commercial farming"
Two developed comparisons (scale, technology, surplus/market), each with a consequence for food security, then a judgement: which performs better under drought, and what the trade-off is (yield vs cost, self-sufficiency vs dependency).
chunks.heading: 2. Types of farming — a spectrum, not three boxes

chunks.text:
Common marks lost
- Mixing systems — putting "rent" in the ecosystem or "sunlight" in the economic system.
- Describing farming types without linking to productivity or food security.
- Value-judgement without mechanism ("farming is bad for the environment").
- Ignoring the binding constraint — students describe what could change, not what is actually limiting yield.
chunks.heading: 2. Types of farming — a spectrum, not three boxes

chunks.text:
1. Sort: fertiliser, rent, sunlight, manager's skill, irrigation water, loan interest — ecosystem or economic system? Justify each.
2. Why does the same word "labour" need two different explanations in an exam?
3. Explain how a shift from subsistence to commercial farming reduces famine risk — give the chain of causes.
4. State one way organic farming is weaker than conventional, and one way it is stronger.
5. In a semi-arid region, identify the binding constraint and explain why adding capital alone won't raise yield.

Source notes: CP5_Combating_Famine_Detailed_Notes · index DSE_SUMMARY · 5.2 Sahel Region (F6 Revision) · 5.6 Sustainable Agriculture (F6 Revision)
chunks.heading: Quick self-check

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
The Sahel is the syllabus's famine-belt case study. Questions nearly always ask you to separate physical from human causes and then weigh which dominates — so build the two lists separately, then argue their interaction.
chunks.heading: 5.2 Sahel Region — F6 Revision

chunks.text:
Location — a semi-arid band immediately south of the Sahara, running across Mauritania, Mali, Niger, Chad and Sudan. Its position between desert and savanna is the source of its vulnerability: it sits on the margin where rainfall becomes unreliable.

Climate
- Semi-arid, roughly 100–400 mm per year — below or at the edge of what reliable rain-fed cropping needs.
- High temperature year-round → high evapotranspiration, so effective moisture is even lower than the rainfall suggests.
- Frequent, unpredictable drought — the rainfall total is less dangerous than its variability: years of plenty, then failure.
- High year-to-year variation — makes planning impossible and prevents surplus accumulation.

Degradation problems
- Desertification — the desert edge advances as vegetation cover is lost.
- Soil erosion — wind on bare ground and sheet wash in short storms remove the fertile layer.
- Water scarcity — rivers and shallow wells fall; groundwater is slow to recharge.
- Nutrient depletion — harvested crops remove nutrients that are not replaced, so yields fall even in good years.
chunks.heading: 1. Physical environment

chunks.text:
- Rapid population growth — more mouths and more land needed per household; output per person falls even if total output rises.
- Traditional farming methods — low input, low yield, no buffer; fallow periods shorten as land gets divided.
- Overgrazing — stocking numbers exceed carrying capacity → vegetation stripped → soil exposed.
- Deforestation — trees cut for fuel and to clear land → windbreaks lost, erosion accelerated, rainfall cycle disrupted.
- Poverty — cannot buy fertiliser, irrigation, seed or insurance, so cannot escape the low-yield trap.
- Limited infrastructure — no roads to move surplus to deficit areas, no storage → food exists but cannot reach hunger.
- Political instability and debt — conflict and fiscal pressure divert spending from agriculture and relief.
chunks.heading: 2. Human factors (the amplifier)

chunks.text:
Answer structure for "Explain why the Sahel is prone to famine / evaluate physical vs human causes"
1. Physical: low, variable rainfall + high evapotranspiration → unreliable yields (mechanism in two steps).
2. Human: population growth, overgrazing, deforestation → degradation → yields fall further.
3. Interaction (the top band): physical conditions set the exposure; human actions determine the severity. Drought alone is a hazard; drought + degraded soil + no storage + no transport becomes famine.
4. Verdict: human factors are the more actionable, physical factors the more unavoidable — state which you judge dominant and why.

Common marks lost
- Listing causes without mechanism — "desertification" named, never explained.
- Treating the Sahel as the Sahara: it is the marginal band, not desert.
- No interaction argument — physical/human lists with nothing connecting them.
- Confusing drought (a hazard) with famine (a food-system failure) — they are not synonyms.
- Missing infrastructure: famine is often about distribution, not total production.
chunks.heading: 2. Human factors (the amplifier)

chunks.text:
1. Explain how 100–400 mm of rainfall becomes a food-security problem through two separate mechanisms.
2. Why does high temperature worsen rainfall scarcity?
3. Trace the chain: overgrazing → vegetation loss → soil erosion → lower yield.
4. Distinguish drought from famine in one sentence each, then state how one leads to the other.
5. Give one case where the Sahel had enough food produced but people still went hungry — what failed?

Source notes: CP5_Combating_Famine_Detailed_Notes · index DSE_SUMMARY · 5.4 Famine Causes & Characteristics (F6 Revision) · Common Mistakes in CP5 concepts
chunks.heading: Quick self-check

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
Southern California is the MDC farming counter-case to the Sahel: a highly productive region where the constraints are environmental (water) rather than poverty. The examiner's favourite task is compare — so keep the structure parallel to 5.2 Sahel Region (F6 Revision).
chunks.heading: 5.3 Southern California — F6 Revision

chunks.text:
Advantages
- Mediterranean climate — dry, sunny summers with a wet winter: warm growing season with no summer rainfall stress provided water is supplied; low humidity also reduces fungal crop disease.
- High sunshine / radiation — strong photosynthesis → high yields and good fruit quality; long growing season allows multiple harvests.
- Fertile soil — alluvial deposits on valley floors and fans from rivers carrying eroded material; naturally high nutrient status.
- Irrigation water from the Colorado River — the single factor that converts an arid climate into one of the world's most productive agricultural regions (it also imports water from hundreds of km away, which is the vulnerability).

Challenges
- Water scarcity — rainfall insufficient in the growing season; supply depends on distant, over-allocated rivers.
- Arid climate — high evapotranspiration means applied water is lost quickly; droughts recur.
- Soil salinity — irrigation raises the water table; evaporation leaves salts in the topsoil → yields fall. (See Common Mistakes in CP5 concepts for the step-by-step salinisation mechanism and the saline soil / salinisation distinction.)
chunks.heading: 1. Physical factors

chunks.text:
- Advanced technology — mechanisation, controlled-environment growing, monitoring; raises yield per hectare and per worker.
- Irrigation systems — drip and sprinkler networks make precise water application possible; technology is what turns the physical advantage into production.
- Capital investment — funds for equipment, cold storage, processing and transport to distant markets.
- Government support — water infrastructure, subsidies, research and regulation.
- Research institutions — universities and agricultural research develop varieties and techniques (bred for heat, disease, market) — this is the classic external economy of scale for a farming region.

Answer structure for "Compare the Sahel with Southern California" / "Explain productivity differences"
1. Compare on matched axes: climate & water, soil, technology & capital, markets/infrastructure.
2. For each axis, give the mechanism and name the binding constraint in each region (Sahel: rainfall variability; S. California: water supply).
3. Note the deep similarity: both are limited by water — one lacks it entirely, the other must import it. The difference is capital and technology, not climate luck.
4. Verdict: which region's agriculture is more sustainable, and why (dependency on imported water vs dependency on rainfall)?
chunks.heading: 2. Human factors

chunks.text:
Common marks lost
- Calling Southern California "wet" — its summers are dry; irrigation is doing the work.
- Listing technology without mechanism ("modern technology helps").
- Explaining salinisation in one clause — examiners want the sequence: irrigation → water table rises → evaporation → salts accumulate → osmotic damage → yield falls.
- No comparison — two descriptions side by side with no matched axes.
- Ignoring that irrigation imports the problem: Colorado River over-allocation is a genuine sustainability limit.
chunks.heading: 2. Human factors

chunks.text:
1. Explain why a dry summer is an advantage for crop quality, then state what it costs.
2. Give the four-step mechanism of soil salinisation and one way to prevent it.
3. Which single human factor would you add to the Sahel to raise yield most — and why does it work in California?
4. Compare the binding constraint in the Sahel with that in Southern California.
5. Is Southern California agriculture sustainable? Argue both sides, then judge.

Source notes: CP5_Combating_Famine_Detailed_Notes · index DSE_SUMMARY · Common Mistakes in CP5 concepts · 5.6 Sustainable Agriculture (F6 Revision)

docs.title: 5.4 Famine — Causes & Characteristics (F6 Revision)
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP5/Concepts/5.4 Famine Causes & Characteristics (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
"Why do famines occur?" is the single most reliable CP5 question. The top band depends on two distinctions: hazard vs famine, and trigger vs root cause.
chunks.heading: 5.4 Famine — Causes & Characteristics (F6 Revision)

chunks.text:
A severe shortage of food causing widespread hunger and death.

Note what the definition implies: famine is about access and distribution, not only total tonnage. A region can produce food and still starve if people cannot buy, move or receive it.
chunks.heading: 1. Definition

chunks.text:
These recur in nearly every case — learn them as a diagnostic checklist:

1. Semi-arid regions — low, unreliable rainfall: output swings wildly year to year.
2. Limited resources and poor infrastructure — no roads, storage or markets, so surplus can't move and deficit can't be reached.
3. Economic problems — poverty and debt: no purchasing power, no buffer, no insurance, debt servicing diverts spending from food.
4. Political problems — conflict and instability: displacement, aid blocked, farms abandoned, governance of reserves fails.
5. Environmental degradation — deforestation and soil erosion reduce the land's carrying capacity, so the same weather now produces less food than it used to.

The pattern to spot: each characteristic both raises the chance of crop failure and removes a buffer against it. That double action is why famine-prone areas are trapped.
chunks.heading: 2. Characteristics of famine-prone areas

chunks.text:
Natural causes (usually the trigger)
- Drought — the classic trigger: a run of failed rains cuts yield sharply.
- Floods — wash away topsoil, seed and standing crop; silt and waterlogging damage land.
- Pest outbreaks — locusts, rusts, blight destroy crops rapidly and across borders.
- Climate variability — the underlying pattern: unpredictable onset and intensity of rains makes planting decisions a gamble.

Human causes (usually the root cause and the severity multiplier)
- War and conflict — destroys farms, kills/livestock, blocks aid, displaces farmers from planting seasons.
- Rapid population growth — more consumers; smaller plots per household; soil rested for shorter periods.
- Land degradation — erosion, salinisation, deforestation → progressively lower yields (a slow-onset cause).
- Poor governance — corruption or mismanagement of reserves, price controls that discourage supply, delayed warnings.
- Trade policies — export of food during shortage, or tariffs/price policy that keeps food unaffordable domestically.
chunks.heading: 3. Causes — separate trigger from root cause

chunks.text:
Answer structure for "Explain why famine occurs in X"
1. State the trigger (one natural cause, with mechanism: "failed rains reduced rain-fed yield by …").
2. Show the root causes that turn shortfall into famine: infrastructure, poverty, governance, conflict.
3. Make the explicit argument: a physical hazard becomes famine only when the food system cannot respond — with one sentence of evidence (storage, roads, purchasing power).
4. Conclude which is more decisive for prevention — because that determines the policy.

Common marks lost
- Using drought and famine interchangeably.
- Only natural causes listed → lands mid-band; human causes are where the marks are.
- No mechanism for any cause ("floods damage crops" — how, and what happens next?).
- Ignoring distribution: food aid exists but cannot reach people.
- No named case (Sahel required by the syllabus).
chunks.heading: 3. Causes — separate trigger from root cause

chunks.text:
1. In one sentence each: hazard, trigger, root cause, famine.
2. Explain how debt contributes to famine without any crop failure at all.
3. Why does poor infrastructure matter twice — at the moment of failure and after it?
4. Give a natural and a human cause, and show how they interact in one region.
5. A country exports food during a shortage. Explain, with mechanisms, how policy can cause famine.

Source notes: CP5_Combating_Famine_Detailed_Notes · index DSE_SUMMARY · 5.2 Sahel Region (F6 Revision) · 5.5 Combating Famine Solutions (F6 Revision)

docs.title: 5.5 Combating Famine — Solutions (F6 Revision)
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP5/Concepts/5.5 Combating Famine Solutions (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
Solutions questions are evaluative by design: "To what extent can short-term measures solve famine?" or "Can GM crops solve world hunger?" The distinction examiners reward is relief vs development — one buys time, the other removes the cause.
chunks.heading: 5.5 Combating Famine — Solutions (F6 Revision)

chunks.text:
Emergency relief
- Food aid — immediate calorie supply; mechanism: bypasses a failed harvest. Limits: arrives after the peak, undercuts local farmers' prices (so the next harvest is damaged), depends on logistics and security.
- Water supply — tankers, wells, purification: prevents dehydration and water-borne disease, which is what often kills after the food shortage.
- Medical care — treats malnutrition and disease; hunger weakens immunity, so disease epidemics follow famine.
- Refugee support / camps — concentrates vulnerable people where aid can reach them; costs host regions and can create dependency.

Food supply management
- Food imports — raise national availability quickly; cost: foreign exchange, shipping time, price exposure.
- Emergency reserves — strategic stock released when prices spike; needs holding cost and honest management.
- Price controls — keep food affordable; risk: discourage supply, create black markets, so the policy can worsen availability.

The key judgement: short-term measures reduce mortality but do nothing about the cause. Repeat the cycle without development.
chunks.heading: 1. Short-term measures (relief — buys time)

chunks.text:
Agricultural development
- Irrigation — decouples production from rainfall variability (the Sahel's binding constraint).
- Drought-resistant crops — raise the yield floor in poor years, which matters more than peak yield.
- Fertilisers and improved seed — restore soil nutrients, lift productivity.
- Modern technology — mechanisation, monitoring, training: raises yield and reduces post-harvest loss.

Infrastructure
- Roads — link farms to markets; move surplus to deficit areas during failure.
- Storage — grain stores/silos prevent spoilage and let surplus be held across bad years (directly attacks year-to-year variability).
- Markets — give farmers price information and an incentive to grow surplus.
- Water systems — rivers, dams, wells: supply and flood/drought moderation.

Economic & social development
- Education — better farming practice, family planning, and ability to read warnings/prices.
- Healthcare — reduces the disease burden that converts malnutrition into death.
- Job creation and trade — purchasing power: famine is as much an income problem as a production problem.
chunks.heading: 2. Long-term solutions (development — removes the cause)

chunks.text:
For: higher yields; pest resistance (less crop loss); drought tolerance (stability in bad years); nutritional enhancement (e.g. fortified staple). Each point needs a mechanism: pest resistance → fewer plants lost → higher effective yield.

Against: uncertain health effects (long-term, disputed — say "contested", don't assert harm); dependency on corporations (patented seed, annual purchase, market power); environmental risk (gene flow to wild relatives, effect on non-target species); loss of traditional seed varieties (genetic diversity that future breeding needs).

Answer structure for "Can X solve famine?"
1. Define what "solve" requires — sustained food availability, access and stability.
2. Show what the measure delivers (mechanism + evidence).
3. Show what it does not address (e.g. food aid doesn't fix infrastructure; GM doesn't fix conflict or purchasing power).
4. Compare short-term vs long-term explicitly, then judge: necessary but not sufficient is usually the defensible verdict — with the condition that would make it sufficient.
chunks.heading: 3. GM crops — the set-piece debate

chunks.text:
Common marks lost
- Treating relief as a solution rather than a stopgap.
- GM debate asserted instead of argued — one-sided answers cap at mid-band.
- No mechanism ("irrigation helps" — why, and which constraint does it remove?).
- Ignoring cost, sustainability or local capacity — evaluative questions award marks for feasibility.
- No case reference (Sahel, Southern California) to anchor the argument.
chunks.heading: 3. GM crops — the set-piece debate

chunks.text:
1. Distinguish emergency relief from agricultural development using one measure each, with mechanism.
2. Explain two ways storage reduces famine risk beyond simply holding food.
3. Why can food aid damage the next season's local production?
4. Give two arguments for and two against GM crops, each with a mechanism.
5. A donor may fund one long-term project only: irrigation, roads, or education. Which do you choose for the Sahel — defend with two mechanisms.

Source notes: CP5_Combating_Famine_Detailed_Notes · index DSE_SUMMARY · 5.4 Famine Causes & Characteristics (F6 Revision) · 5.6 Sustainable Agriculture (F6 Revision)
chunks.heading: Quick self-check

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
Sustainable agriculture is where CP5 joins CP4 — the same three-pillar test applied to farming. Data-response items regularly use the organic farming table in your source notes, so practise reading it and drawing cautious conclusions.
chunks.heading: 5.6 Sustainable Agriculture — F6 Revision

chunks.text:
Environmental — conserve resources (soil, water, biodiversity), reduce pollution (agrochemicals, runoff), protect ecosystems.
- Mechanism: soil is a non-renewable asset on human timescales — farming that mines soil fertility yields more this decade and less the next.

Economic — must remain profitable and efficient, and respond to markets.
- Mechanism: a farm that cannot cover costs abandons the practice; sustainability that isn't affordable doesn't persist.

Social — fair labour conditions, community benefit, food security.
- Mechanism: farming systems that destabilise rural communities (or price food out of reach) fail the pillar even if yields are high.

The examinable tension: environmental measures often lower yield or raise cost short-term; economic pressure pushes the other way. Sustainable agriculture is the balance point, and questions ask you to locate it.
chunks.heading: 1. Principles — the three-pillar test for farming

chunks.text:
- Crop rotation — alternate crops across seasons: different species draw different nutrients and host different pests → soil nutrients maintained and pest cycles broken, reducing fertiliser and pesticide need. Also breaks disease carry-over.
- Organic farming — natural fertilisers (compost, manure) and no synthetic pesticides → no chemical runoff, better soil structure and organisms. Cost: lower yields, more labour, more knowledge, and produce must fetch a premium to remain economic.
- Agroforestry — trees integrated with crops/livestock: shade and shelter reduce heat/wind stress and water loss; multiple outputs (fruit, timber, fodder, crops) spread income risk; roots hold soil.
- Water management — drip irrigation delivers water to roots with minimal evaporation (critical where water is scarce); rainwater harvesting stores wet-season water for dry-season use; recycling/treated reuse reduces demand on freshwater. Each attacks a specific loss pathway rather than just "saving water".
chunks.heading: 2. Practices — mechanism for each

chunks.text:
| Country | Organic area (M ha) | Share (%) | Income/capita (USD) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Australia | 12.3 | 2.8 | 34,923 |
| Brazil | 0.9 | 0.3 | 9,567 |
| USA | 1.6 | 0.5 | 45,592 |
| China | 2.3 | 0.4 | 5,383 |
| Italy | 1.1 | 9.0 | 30,353 |
| UK | 0.6 | 3.8 | 35,130 |

What the table actually supports
- Absolute area is led by Australia (land availability), but share is led by Italy (9.0%) — so "who leads" depends on which measure you choose. Say which you are using.
- Higher-income countries generally show higher shares (Italy, UK) — consistent with consumers paying a premium and with stricter regulation/market maturity.
- China's large area but tiny share (0.4%) shows a large agricultural sector with little organic conversion.
- The source notes also record: the USA resists large-scale adoption because of lower yields and higher costs — the economic-pillar objection in one line.

Careful reading: correlation with income ≠ causation; and land area ≠ share. Examiners award the distinction.
chunks.heading: 3. The organic farming case data (and how to read it)

chunks.text:
Answer structure for "Evaluate sustainable agriculture measures"
1. Name 2–3 practices with mechanism (rotation, drip irrigation, agroforestry).
2. Judge each against the three pillars — environmental gain, economic cost, social effect.
3. Use one piece of evidence (the organic table, or a named region).
4. Conclude with the condition for success: premium markets, water savings, or policy support — whichever the mechanism requires.

Common marks lost
- Practices listed with no mechanism or no evaluation.
- Quoting organic yields as "worse" without the market/premium context.
- Claiming organic = sustainable by definition — it can fail the economic pillar.
- Mixing CP4 urban language into a farming question.
- Reading the table loosely (area vs share confusion).
chunks.heading: 3. The organic farming case data (and how to read it)

chunks.text:
1. Explain how crop rotation reduces fertiliser use — the mechanism, not the label.
2. Give one economic and one environmental argument against expanding organic farming.
3. Using the table, state which country leads on area and which on share, and why the difference matters.
4. Why is drip irrigation more sustainable than flood irrigation in an arid region?
5. Apply the three pillars to agroforestry: one gain and one cost for each pillar.

Source notes: CP5_Combating_Famine_Detailed_Notes · index DSE_SUMMARY · Common Mistakes in CP5 concepts · 5.3 Southern California (F6 Revision) · 4.1 Sustainable Development (F6 Revision)
chunks.heading: Quick self-check

chunks.text:
Draft for review
Each item: place + year · what happened with a hard number · the CP5 concept it illustrates · source. Numbers came from searches on 2026-09-27 — spot-check any you intend to put in front of students.
chunks.heading: CP5 Update Cases 2025–2026 — Combating Famine

chunks.text:
- Sudan — Darfur/Kordofan, Sep 2025. IPC confirmed Famine (Phase 5) in El Fasher (North Darfur) and Kadugli (South Kordofan); 21.2 million people (45%) in IPC Phase 3+, including 375,000 in Catastrophe; malnutrition above the 30% famine threshold in 4 Greater Darfur localities. Conflict + siege + aid blockade. — IPC Famine Review Committee Report, Sudan, Oct 2025.
- Gaza Strip, Aug–Sep 2025. First IPC-confirmed famine in the Middle East: ~641,000 in Phase 5; ~98% of cropland damaged or inaccessible; 12,000+ children acutely malnourished in July (six-fold rise since January). Man-made famine, collapse of local agriculture. — WHO/FAO/UNICEF/WFP IPC analysis, 22 Aug 2025.
- Sahel / West & Central Africa, 2025 lean season. 52 million people in Cadre Harmonisé Phase 3+ across 13 countries (Nigeria 30.6 m, Chad 3.3 m, Niger 2.2 m, Mali 1.5 m); 2,600 in Catastrophe in Ménaka/Tessalit, Mali; staple-cereal prices 10–200% above the 5-year average. Conflict + climate + price inflation. — CILSS/PREGEC, March 2025.
- South Sudan, Sept 2025–July 2026. 5.97 million in Phase 3+ (42%); 28,000 in Phase 5 Catastrophe (17,000 Luakpiny/Nasir, 11,000 Fangak); Luakpiny/Nasir at risk of Famine. Protracted conflict + refugee return from Sudan. — IPC South Sudan Snapshot, Sept 2025.
- Yemen, May 2025–Feb 2026. 17.1 million (49%) in Phase 3+, projected 18.1 million (52%) by Feb 2026, 41,000 in Phase 5 (Hajjah, Al Hodeidah, Amran); food assistance cut from 3.6 m recipients (2024) to zero from July 2025. Failure of combating measures — aid cuts drive famine. — IPC Yemen Special Brief, 27 June 2025.
chunks.heading: Causes of famine

chunks.text:
- Horn of Africa (Somalia, Kenya, Ethiopia), Dec 2025. Historic failed Oct–Nov rains: 20–25 million need food assistance; Somalia's Bay/Bakool non-irrigated harvest projected <10% of average; maize +19% above the 5-year average (Kitui), red sorghum +25% (Baidoa); livestock milk down about one-third (Mandera). — FEWS NET East Africa Alert, 23 Dec 2025.
- Europe, June 2026 heatwave. Record June heat cut the EU+UK grain harvest by 9 million tonnes (lowest since 2018), about €2 bn lost revenue; France −3.4 m t of maize, Hungary −2.4 m t, Spain −1.4 m t. Climate shock to staple crops in industrial agriculture. — The Guardian, 22 July 2026 (Coceral/ECIU).
- Pakistan — Indus Plains, 2022 monsoon floods. 2.67 million acres (13.3%) of Punjab cropland and 287,000 ha (16.5%) of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa cultivable land inundated; 15% of Punjab's rice region submerged; major crops = 81.2% of total agricultural losses. Flood-driven crop failure. — Springer, "Assessing Agrometeorological Damage after the 2022 Pakistan Floods", 2025.

- Causes → 5.4 Famine Causes & Characteristics (F6 Revision)
- Combating measures → 5.5 Combating Famine Solutions (F6 Revision)
- Sustainable agriculture → 5.6 Sustainable Agriculture (F6 Revision)
