docs.title: 7.2 The Greenhouse Effect (F6 Revision)
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP7/Concepts/7.2 The Greenhouse Effect (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why this is on the paper
The greenhouse effect is the module's core mechanism, and the examiner's standing trap is the natural versus enhanced distinction. Candidates who explain "the greenhouse effect" once, vaguely, and then apply it to everything score mid-band at best. The top band requires you to show the same mechanism working at two different intensities and to explain what the difference does to outgoing radiation.
chunks.heading: 7.2 The Greenhouse Effect (F6 Revision)

chunks.text:
Stage 1 — the surface emits. Sunlight warms the Earth's surface, which then emits energy as longwave (infrared) radiation.

Stage 2 — the atmosphere absorbs and re-emits. Greenhouse gases — carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, water vapour and the synthetic halocarbons — absorb that outgoing longwave radiation, which in turn reduces the rate at which energy escapes to space. They then re-emit it in all directions, including back down to the surface.

Two consequences follow, and both must be in your answer:

1. The surface is warmed by energy arriving from below as well as from above, so its temperature is higher than it would be with no atmosphere.
2. The atmosphere is warmed from below by the longwave it absorbs, so it also has a higher temperature than it would otherwise have.

This is why the effect is called a greenhouse effect only by analogy. A real greenhouse works by trapping air so that warm air cannot convect away; the atmospheric greenhouse effect works by absorbing and re-emitting infrared radiation. Examiners know the difference and reward the candidate who does not confuse them.
chunks.heading: 1. The mechanism in two stages

chunks.text:
Without any greenhouse effect, Earth's mean surface temperature would be roughly −18 °C instead of about +15 °C — the difference between a frozen planet and a habitable one. Water vapour is the most important greenhouse gas by volume in the natural system, followed by carbon dioxide and then methane; the small but industrially produced gases (CFCs, HFCs, HCFCs and SF₆) contribute disproportionately to warming because they are potent and long-lived.

What the natural effect does for the planet:

- Keeps the surface temperature above freezing, so liquid water exists and the hydrological cycle works.
- Keeps oceans liquid enough to sustain marine ecosystems and the global thermohaline circulation.
- Makes the global temperature gradient between the equator and the poles gentle enough for a single species to occupy most of the planet.
- Provides the longwave "blanket" that keeps the temperature contrast between day and night, and between seasons, from becoming extreme.
chunks.heading: 2. The natural greenhouse effect is not optional

chunks.text:
The point to make explicitly: the natural greenhouse effect is not the cause of climate change. It is the baseline condition against which the enhanced effect operates. The scientific debate in CP7 is never "is there a greenhouse effect?" — it is "is the greenhouse effect changing, and why?"
The named comparison: Venus and Mars. Venus has a surface temperature of about 465 °C, hotter than Mercury despite being further from the Sun, because its dense carbon dioxide atmosphere traps outgoing longwave radiation with no effective way to lose heat. Mars, with a thin carbon dioxide atmosphere, is cold. The pair is the standard proof that the greenhouse effect, not distance from the Sun, sets a planet's surface temperature — and it is the template the examiner expects when asking about the enhanced greenhouse effect on Earth.
chunks.heading: 2. The natural greenhouse effect is not optional

chunks.text:
The enhanced greenhouse effect is the strengthening of the natural effect by human activity. Write it as a chain, because each link is a mark:

1. Human activities — burning fossil fuels, deforestation, industrial processes, some agriculture — release additional greenhouse gases into the atmosphere.
2. Atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide therefore rise above their natural range.
3. With more of these gases, a larger fraction of outgoing longwave radiation is absorbed before it can escape through the atmospheric window.
4. The re-emitted energy returns downwards, so the surface and lower atmosphere gain energy.
5. The planet is therefore out of balance — more energy in than out — and the surplus is stored as heat in the ocean, the atmosphere and the cryosphere.
6. Global temperatures rise, which feeds back into changes in the water cycle, ice cover and circulation.

Why step 3 is the one that matters. Note what has not changed: the Sun's output, the Earth's orbit, the total amount of sunlight arriving. The change is entirely in the efficiency with which the Earth loses energy to space. That is why the natural greenhouse effect being "good" and the enhanced one being "bad" is not a contradiction — they differ only in quantity, and quantity controls the outgoing term.
chunks.heading: 3. The enhanced greenhouse effect: the causal chain

chunks.text:
Once the mechanism is understood, feedbacks are where the extra marks live.

Positive feedbacks (self-amplifying — these make matters worse)

- Ice-albedo feedback. Warming melts snow and ice → dark ocean and land absorb more shortwave → more warming → more melt. Arctic amplification follows from the same logic: losing reflective sea ice exposes dark ocean water, which in turn warms faster than the ice did.
- Water vapour feedback. Warmer air holds more moisture → more water vapour, itself a greenhouse gas → more warming → more moisture.
- Permafrost carbon feedback. Warming thaws permafrost → organic matter decomposes → releases carbon dioxide and methane → more warming → more thaw.
- Fire feedback. Drier, hotter conditions raise wildfire risk in some regions → more smoke and more carbon released → less vegetation to absorb carbon → more warming.

Negative feedbacks (self-limiting — these push back)
chunks.heading: 4. Feedbacks: the examiner's favourite extension

chunks.text:
- Cloud response. Some cloud types reflect incoming sunlight; their behaviour in a warmer world partly offsets warming, though the size of the cloud feedback remains an active research area.
- Increased ocean heat uptake. The ocean absorbs most of the surplus heat, which slows atmospheric warming — but it also causes thermal expansion and delays the benefit of cuts.
- Vegetation response. Higher temperatures can boost plant growth where water is not limiting, removing some carbon — though where drought follows heat, the effect reverses.

How to use feedbacks in an answer: they explain why the temperature curve is accelerating rather than linear, and why stopping emissions does not immediately stop warming. Never write a feedback without the loop closed: "warming → … → warming".
chunks.heading: 4. Feedbacks: the examiner's favourite extension

chunks.text:
- Sea level rise is a downstream consequence: warming increases ocean heat content, which makes seawater expand, and it melts land ice, which adds water. Both are energy-balance outcomes, not separate processes.
- Extreme weather follows because a warmer atmosphere holds about 7 per cent more moisture per degree of warming, so the same storm system can deliver more intense rainfall.
- Policy follows from the same chain: because the mechanism is more greenhouse gas, mitigation means less greenhouse gas — carbon pricing, renewables, efficiency, afforestation — while adaptation deals with the consequences.
chunks.heading: 5. Consequences for other parts of the module

chunks.text:
- Explain the greenhouse effect: surface emits longwave → greenhouse gases absorb → re-emit in all directions including downwards → surface and atmosphere warm → and the natural effect keeps Earth habitable.
- Explain the enhanced greenhouse effect: add the human source → rising concentrations → more longwave absorbed → more energy returned downwards → energy surplus stored → warming.
- Compare natural with enhanced: the mechanism is identical; only the quantity of greenhouse gas and therefore the size of the outgoing term differ. Say this explicitly — it is the mark.
- "Evaluate the view that the greenhouse effect is entirely beneficial": accept the natural effect's benefits, then show that the enhanced effect works on the same lever and the benefits do not scale — beyond a threshold, extra greenhouse gas makes things worse rather than better.
chunks.heading: Answer structure

chunks.text:
- "The greenhouse effect traps heat like the glass of a car." Wrong mechanism. The atmospheric effect is absorption and re-emission of longwave radiation, not trapping of air.
- Conflating the natural and enhanced effects, or writing "the greenhouse effect is causing global warming" without saying which effect.
- Saying the Sun's output has increased. The energy imbalance is on the outgoing side.
- Writing "heat cannot escape" — energy conservation is not broken; the rate of escape is reduced and part of the energy is redirected downwards.
- Listing feedbacks without closing the loop. "Ice melts, more warming" is a fragment; "ice melts → the darker surface absorbs more shortwave radiation → more warming → more ice melts" is a mechanism.
- Forgetting the ocean. A candidate who puts all the surplus heat in the atmosphere has the wrong budget: the ocean has taken up more than 90 per cent of the excess heat since 1970.
chunks.heading: Common marks lost

chunks.text:
1. Write the greenhouse effect as a three-step chain, and say which step the enhanced effect changes.
2. Why would the Earth's mean surface temperature be about −18 °C without an atmosphere?
3. Explain the ice-albedo feedback, closing the loop.
4. A warming planet's atmosphere holds about 7 per cent more moisture per degree. What follows for heavy rainfall?
5. Why does the natural greenhouse effect not prevent the enhanced effect from occurring?
6. Give one positive and one negative feedback, and say which one is currently thought to dominate.

docs.title: 7.20 The Need for Adaptation (F6 Revision)
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP7/Concepts/7.20 The Need for Adaptation (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why this is on the paper
This leaf supplies the argument that makes the whole mitigation-versus-adaptation section coherent, and it is where the examiner looks for a candidate who can reason about why adaptation is necessary rather than merely listing its benefits. The two claims you must be able to defend: (i) some warming is already inevitable, and (ii) adaptation is limited, so mitigation is not optional. Together they produce the conclusion the module wants: mitigation and adaptation are complements, and adaptation without mitigation eventually becomes unaffordable.
chunks.heading: 7.20 The Need for Adaptation (F6 Revision)

chunks.text:
- The physical inertia of the ocean. The ocean has taken up more than 90 per cent of the excess heat in the climate system since 1970, and the rate of ocean warming since 1993 has more than doubled. Heat already in the upper ocean must be mixed upward, so the surface temperature continues to rise even if emissions stop immediately. The lag is measured in decades.
- The persistence of CO₂. A large fraction of emitted CO₂ is removed only over centuries to millennia. Stopping emissions stops the rise in concentration, but the concentration keeps climbing for decades and then remains elevated far longer.
- The commitment of the cryosphere. Ice sheets respond over centuries to millennia; once mass loss begins it continues even at stable temperature. Sea level therefore has a long memory.
- The conclusion. Because CO₂ and the ocean heat are effectively irreversible on any human planning horizon, a portion of warming is already locked in. This is a physical statement, not a policy opinion, and it is the foundation of the case for adaptation.
chunks.heading: 1. Why some warming is inevitable

chunks.text:
- Adaptation has limits, and the limits scale with the amount of warming. The National Academies' framing of the "adaptation gap" — the difference between the adaptation that is possible and the adaptation that is needed — widens as warming increases. When the sea level rises far enough, no seawall is feasible; when heat exceeds the survivable range, no warning system helps.
- Some impacts are not adaptable at all. The loss of an island's land, the extinction of a species, and the abandonment of a settlement are not adaptations, they are losses. The Tuvalu case is the honest limit case.
- Cost. Adaptation is expensive and must be repeated as the baseline shifts — the same seawall must be raised as the sea level rises. Mitigation reduces the number of times adaptation has to be done.
- Timing. Adaptation is often politically easier than mitigation because its benefits are local, visible and immediate, which in turn makes it attractive — and it is also why adaptation alone is dangerous: it defers the harder, more expensive, more globally coordinated decision.
- The decisive argument. Mitigation determines the scale of the adaptation problem. Every fraction of a degree avoided means less sea level rise, less heat, less adaptation expenditure and fewer limits crossed. Adaptation manages the warming that mitigation failed to prevent; mitigation reduces the adaptation bill.
chunks.heading: 2. Why adaptation cannot substitute for mitigation

chunks.text:
An adaptation measure is effective when it actually reduces loss. The four properties that matter:

1. Robustness — it works across a range of future climate scenarios, not only the "central" projection. This is what the "adaptive delta management" approach used in the Netherlands and adapted in Bangladesh is designed to do.
2. Flexibility — it can be modified as understanding improves, rather than locking the city into one design for a century.
3. Maladaptation avoidance — the measure does not increase risk elsewhere or for someone else. Embankments in Bangladesh that protect the city but worsen flooding in neighbouring districts are maladaptation; so are seawalls that protect a shoreline while destroying the mangrove that was absorbing wave energy.
4. Equity and "leaving no-one behind" — the measure protects those most at risk, not just those who can pay. Bangladesh's Delta Plan 2100 explicitly rejects the goal of making Bangladesh flood-free, because that is neither feasible nor desirable, and adopts instead the goal of mitigating the most undesired effects and enabling rapid recovery.
chunks.heading: 3. What makes adaptation effective

chunks.text:
- Adaptation is not a separate activity from development. Almost every adaptation measure — drainage, housing, water supply, transport, early warning — is also a development investment. This is the argument for treating adaptation finance as development finance rather than as charity.
- The "maladaptation" risk in development. Unplanned urbanisation into floodplains and hazard zones creates a development problem that then requires much larger adaptation expenditure later. Preventing the problem through land-use regulation is cheaper than coping with it.
- Hong Kong's example. The Harbourfront and Kai Tak developments, the drainage improvement works and the coastal protection schemes around Victoria Harbour and the New Territories are simultaneously development projects and adaptation measures.
chunks.heading: 4. The adaptation–development link

chunks.text:
- The asymmetry. Adaptation is funded largely by the countries that need it, while mitigation is a global responsibility; the international system has historically channelled more money to mitigation than to adaptation, and mitigation finance goes to countries that can repay it.
- The COP30 outcome. At COP30 in Belém in November 2025, the Parties adopted the Belém Package, which triples adaptation finance by 2035 and launched the Baku Adaptation Roadmap 2026–2028. This is a significant signal that the imbalance is being recognised.
- COP29's new finance goal — at least USD 300 billion per year by 2035, replacing the USD 100 billion goal, with an ambition of USD 1.3 trillion from all sources — was accepted amid strong objection, with India calling it a "paltry sum". The dispute is not just about the total; it is about whether the money is mitigation finance or adaptation finance, and about who controls it.
chunks.heading: 5. The finance dimension

chunks.text:
- "Explain why adaptation is necessary": some warming is locked in → the ocean heat, CO₂ persistence and cryosphere commitment → therefore impacts will continue and increase even with aggressive mitigation.
- "Assess the view that adaptation is a better response than mitigation": argue that adaptation's benefits are immediate and local while mitigation's are delayed and global; then rebut with the adaptation gap, the unadaptable impacts, the repeated cost, and the fact that mitigation sets the size of the adaptation bill.
- "Explain why some impacts cannot be adapted to": loss of land, species extinction, settlement abandonment — the honest limits, which is what makes Tuvalu's case powerful.
- "Evaluate the effectiveness of adaptation measures": use robustness, flexibility, maladaptation avoidance and equity as the criteria, then judge one case against them.
- "Discuss the relationship between adaptation and development": shared measures, the maladaptation risk of poorly planned development, and why adaptation finance should be treated as development finance.
chunks.heading: Answer structure

chunks.text:
- Treating adaptation as a free alternative to mitigation. The module's position is that they are complements.
- Not explaining why some warming is inevitable — the ocean and the cryosphere are the answer, and they are exactly what the examiner wants.
- Failing to mention the adaptation gap and the idea that adaptation limits scale with warming.
- Ignoring maladaptation, which is the sophisticated point about adaptation.
- Treating loss and damage as a form of adaptation. Loss and damage finance addresses harm that could neither be prevented nor adapted to.
- Omitting the finance dimension, where the disagreement between developed and developing countries actually happens.
- Forgetting that adaptation is largely local, which is why it can proceed without international agreement while mitigation cannot.
chunks.heading: Common marks lost

chunks.text:
1. Explain why some warming is inevitable, using two physical processes.
2. Define the adaptation gap and explain why it widens.
3. Give two examples of impacts that cannot be adapted to.
4. State four properties that make an adaptation measure effective.
5. Define maladaptation and give one example.
6. Explain in two sentences why mitigation reduces the cost of adaptation.

chunks.text:
Why this is on the paper
Adaptation strategies is where the module becomes a menu of engineering and policy options, and the examiner wants them organised by the hazard they address, each with a mechanism and a limitation. The two marks that separate the bands are (i) the distinction between hard and soft or nature-based measures and the trade-offs between them, and (ii) recognising maladaptation — a measure that reduces risk in one place while creating it in another.
chunks.heading: 7.21 Adaptation Strategies (F6 Revision)

chunks.text:
Before choosing measures, classify the threat, because the strategy follows from it:

| Threat | Character of the strategy | Typical measures |
|---|---|---|
| Sea level rise and storm surge | Slow, predictable, long-term, expensive, cumulative | Seawalls, surge barriers, mangrove restoration, land-use zoning, managed retreat |
| Flooding (river and pluvial) | Episodic, partly predictable, rapid-onset | Embankments, drainage, sponge-city design, flood-proofing, early warning |
| Heatwaves | Episodic, short-duration, high mortality risk | Heat-health warning systems, urban greening, cool roofs, building codes, cool spaces |
| Drought and water scarcity | Slow-onset, structural, chronic | Reservoir expansion, desalination, leak reduction, water saving, drought-tolerant crops, groundwater recharge |
| Cyclones and storms | Episodic, sudden, high-intensity | Early warning, cyclone shelters, building codes for wind loads, coastal belt protection |
| Agricultural disruption | Seasonal, livelihood-based | Drought-resistant varieties, changed planting dates, irrigation, index insurance |
| Coral reef and ecosystem loss | Chronic, slow | Marine protected areas, reducing local stressors, coral restoration, nursery programmes |
chunks.heading: 1. The organising framework: what are you adapting to?

chunks.text:
Hard engineering
- Seawalls and surge barriers. Direct protection of a fixed line. The Maldives is the case: the seawall around Malé, originally built with Japanese grant aid in the late 1980s, protected the capital from the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, and Japan signed a further grant agreement in 2025 for improvements to the seawall and stormwater drainage, with a maximum grant of 1,555 million Japanese yen, and a 2026 contract for renovation of the eastern and northern sections.
- Advantages: certainty of protection for a defined area; protection of dense assets and dense populations; it can be designed to a specified standard.
- Disadvantages: very high capital and maintenance cost; it protects a line but not the hinterland behind it; and it can produce maladaptation by transferring erosion or flooding elsewhere, and by destroying the natural systems that were absorbing wave energy.
chunks.heading: 2. Coastal strategies, and the hard-versus-soft trade-off

chunks.text:
Nature-based ("soft") measures
- Mangrove restoration and coastal wetlands. They dissipate wave energy and reduce storm surge height, they store carbon in sediments (so they are mitigation as well as adaptation), they provide fisheries and nursery habitat, and they are cheaper and self-maintaining.
- Limitations: they take years to establish, so they cannot be the sole defence in the near term; they need space, and that space often competes with development; and they are themselves vulnerable to sea level rise at their landward edge.
- The strongest answer says: hard and soft measures are complements, not alternatives. Soft measures reduce the wave energy hard measures must resist, extending the life of the hard structure and lowering its cost — the "no-regret, nature-based" sequencing the Dutch Delta Programme uses.
chunks.heading: 2. Coastal strategies, and the hard-versus-soft trade-off

chunks.text:
Land-use and managed retreat
- Zoning and hazard mapping to keep new development out of the highest-risk zones is the cheapest adaptation available, because it prevents the problem rather than coping with it — which in turn avoids defending it later.
- Managed retreat — organised relocation away from the hazard — is the strategy for places where protection is not viable. Kiribati's planned relocation to Tebung South on Abaiang island is the standard case, with the South Tarawa (Betio) project protecting and reclaiming land in the intertidal zone.
chunks.heading: 2. Coastal strategies, and the hard-versus-soft trade-off

chunks.text:
- Demand-side measures — leakage reduction, metering, water saving appliances, pricing — are usually the cheapest per unit of water saved and they reduce energy use as well.
- Supply-side measures — reservoir expansion, desalination, rainwater harvesting, groundwater recharge — add capacity but carry environmental costs: reservoirs flood land and disrupt river ecosystems; desalination is energy-intensive and produces brine needing disposal; over-extraction of groundwater causes subsidence, which increases local flood risk and relative sea level.
- Agricultural adaptation — drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant crop varieties, changed planting dates to match new rainfall patterns, irrigation efficiency, and index-based insurance that pays out when rainfall or temperature thresholds are crossed rather than requiring an assessment of crop loss.
- Bangladesh's Bangladesh Delta Plan 2100 (BDP 2100) is the model of a comprehensive national approach, developed with technical assistance from the Netherlands and organised around flood risk management, freshwater supply and spatial adaptation, with an explicit "leaving no-one behind" principle.
chunks.heading: 3. Water and drought

chunks.text:
- Heat-health warning systems — issued by meteorological services and linked to public health advice — are the cheapest and most immediately effective measure. The Hong Kong Observatory issues such warnings and works with the health authorities on heat stress.
- Cooling and shelter — public cool spaces, shaded rest areas, and opening schools and public buildings as cooling centres — directly reduces exposure during a heatwave.
- Urban design — greening, cool roofs, shading, and reducing waste heat from air conditioning and vehicles (see 7.12).
- Building and health-system measures — insulation, passive cooling, and training health workers to recognise heat illness early.
- The equity dimension. Adaptation measures must target those at highest risk — outdoor workers, the elderly, the chronically ill and the poor — which usually means targeted provision rather than city-wide provision.
chunks.heading: 4. Heat and health

chunks.text:
- Climate-smart agriculture: varieties matched to new thermal and moisture conditions, adjusted planting and harvesting dates, improved soil moisture management through cover crops, and diversification of crops so that a single failed season is not a livelihood failure.
- Disaster risk financing: catastrophe bonds, parametric insurance, and national disaster funds, which are what allow a farmer or a city to rebuild after an event without taking on unmanageable debt.
- Ecosystem-based adaptation: protected areas and restored habitats as the buffer between human settlements and hazards; coral nurseries and reef restoration in the Maldives and the Caribbean.
chunks.heading: 5. Agriculture and ecosystems

chunks.text:
The criteria for judging any strategy: effectiveness at reducing loss; cost; equity (does it protect those most at risk?); maladaptation (does it transfer risk elsewhere?); robustness across scenarios; and flexibility as knowledge improves.

The honest limitations to state:
- Hard engineering is expensive and has a finite life, and it must be repeatedly upgraded as the baseline rises. The Dutch Delta Programme is explicitly an ongoing commitment rather than a finished project.
- Nature-based measures need time and space that may not be available where the risk is greatest.
- Relocation is socially devastating even when it is the rational economic answer, because it severs people from place, livelihood and community.
- Adaptation measures can protect assets without protecting people — which raises the classic point about whether the objective is to protect the city or its residents.
- Adaptation is itself a target of climate change. A seawall designed for today's sea level is under-designed tomorrow; a mangrove belt may itself be drowned. Hence the emphasis on adaptive, staged, no-regret design.
chunks.heading: 6. Evaluating adaptation strategies

chunks.text:
- "Explain adaptation strategies for coastal flooding": hard engineering, nature-based measures, land-use planning and managed retreat; for each, the mechanism and the limitation; close on the complementarity of hard and soft.
- "Compare the responses of Tuvalu and the Maldives": both small island states, but Tuvalu's threat is total land loss with a relocation strategy, while the Maldives' threat is more manageable for the capital through hard protection and the threat is concentrated in the tourism economy.
- "Discuss the effectiveness of early warning systems": the Bangladesh CPP and the cyclone shelter network, the mortality reductions they achieve, the requirements (forecast skill, communication, trust, shelter within reach) and the fact that warning alone does nothing without shelter and evacuation capacity.
- "Evaluate adaptation strategies for a small island state": apply the criteria — effectiveness, cost, equity, maladaptation, robustness, flexibility — to each option, and close on the honest point that for the most exposed places, no strategy is sufficient.
- "Explain why land-use planning is the cheapest adaptation measure": because it prevents the exposure rather than coping with it, and the cost of regulating development is far below the cost of defending it later.
chunks.heading: Answer structure

chunks.text:
- Listing measures without a mechanism or a limitation.
- Not distinguishing hard from soft measures, which is the framework the examiner expects.
- Ignoring maladaptation.
- Omitting managed retreat because it is uncomfortable — but it is the honest answer for Tuvalu and Kiribati.
- Forgetting the equity dimension, which the examiner rewards in every adaptation answer.
- Failing to state that adaptation measures themselves expire, which is the link back to 7.20.
- Treating adaptation as costless — capital and maintenance costs are real and recurring.
chunks.heading: Common marks lost

chunks.text:
1. Classify adaptation strategies by the threat they address.
2. Give the advantages and disadvantages of hard coastal engineering, and of nature-based measures.
3. Explain why hard and soft coastal measures are complements.
4. What is maladaptation? Give one example.
5. Explain why relocation may be economically rational and socially devastating.
6. Name four criteria for judging an adaptation strategy.

docs.title: 7.22 Observed Trends in Hong Kong (F6 Revision)
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP7/Concepts/7.22 Observed Trends in Hong Kong (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why this is on the paper
This is the leaf that proves the module is about Hong Kong, and it is where the examiner can check your figures against their own. Hong Kong's data are unusually good — a continuous instrumental record from the Hong Kong Observatory (HKO) going back to 1884 — so a candidate who quotes HKO's own numbers is rewarded. The marks come from a trend with a rate, a period and a mechanism.
chunks.heading: 7.22 Observed Trends in Hong Kong (F6 Revision)

chunks.text:
- The record. The HKO Headquarters has recorded temperature continuously since 1884, with a break during the Second World War (1940–1946).
- The long-term trend. Annual mean temperature rose at about 0.14 °C per decade over 1885–2025.
- The recent trend — and this is the important point. Over 1996–2025 the rate was about 0.35 °C per decade, more than twice the long-run rate. Both trends are statistically significant at the 5 per cent level.
- Why the acceleration matters. A single rate over the whole record understates the current rate of change. A candidate who quotes only the 0.14 °C figure is technically right and substantively misleading, because the relevant baseline for the future is the recent rate.
- The indicator shifts, not just the mean. Hot nights (minimum 28 °C or above) and very hot days (maximum 33 °C or above) have risen sharply, while cold days (minimum 12 °C or below) have fallen, which in turn matters more for health than the mean does. Between 1884–1913 Hong Kong averaged about 0.6 hot nights and 2.2 very hot days a year; over 1996–2025, about 30.1 hot nights and 24.8 very hot days, with cold days down from 29.5 to 14.7.
- The most recent year. 2025 was the sixth warmest on record, with an annual mean of 24.3 °C, about 0.8 °C above the 1991–2020 normal; all twelve months were warmer than usual, and October 2025 had the highest monthly mean temperature ever recorded for October. There were 53 very hot days and 54 hot nights, both third highest on record, and only 6 cold days. It was the first year since the Cold Weather Warning System began in 1999 that no warning was in force in November and December.
chunks.heading: 1. Temperature: the record and the acceleration

chunks.text: The interpretation to write: the indicators that matter most for health are hot nights, because the body needs a cool night to recover; the growth of hot nights, more than the growth of hot days, is what drives heat mortality.
chunks.heading: 1. Temperature: the record and the acceleration

chunks.text:
- Annual rainfall at the HKO Headquarters has increased at about 2.3 mm per year over 1884–2025, statistically significant at the 5 per cent level.
- Heavy rain days (hourly rainfall above 30 mm) have increased at about 0.1 day per decade.
- But the pattern is what matters. A study of 131 years of hourly rainfall found extremes intensified by roughly 29 to 38 per cent between 1885 and 2022, the higher percentiles fastest — the 99.9th percentile rose about 0.12 mm per year against 0.03 mm per year for the 95th. Extreme events increased even as all precipitation events decreased.
- The projection. HKO's projections show no significant trend in the total number of rain days, but extreme rainfall days and average rainfall intensity are both expected to increase.
- The key concept. Total rainfall can stay similar or even increase while the risk of flooding rises sharply, because the rain arrives in fewer, more intense events. This is the most important point in the section — it explains why drainage capacity has to keep improving even though the annual total is not changing dramatically.
chunks.heading: 2. Rainfall: more rain, but in the wrong pattern

chunks.text:
- The record. Tide gauge records at Victoria Harbour since 1954 show an unambiguous rise in mean sea level despite annual variability.
- The rate. The increasing rate of annual mean sea level at Victoria Harbour was about 32 mm per decade over 1954–2025, corrected for land settlement. The comparable figure for 1954–2023 was 31 mm per decade.
- The consequence. Because the baseline has risen, the same storm surge reaches further inland and more often. HKO records a maximum storm-surge sea level in Victoria Harbour of 3.96 m above Chart Datum during Super Typhoon Wanda in 1962.
- The projection. Under a high emissions scenario, sea level near Hong Kong is projected to rise by about 0.63 to 1.07 m by the end of this century (2081–2100) compared with the 1986–2005 average.
- Local subsidence. Hong Kong's land reclamation and the settlement of reclaimed ground add to relative sea level rise locally — a point that distinguishes Hong Kong from the global figure.
chunks.heading: 3. Sea level

chunks.text:
- Hong Kong's urban heat island adds a local surcharge on top of the rising global and regional baseline. The dense, highly built Kowloon peninsula sits within the metro area, with the more open New Territories to the north and east.
- The mechanism is the one set out in 7.12: reduced evapotranspiration, low-albedo high-thermal-mass surfaces, restricted ventilation in street canyons, and anthropogenic heat from air conditioning — near-universal in a subtropical city.
- The interaction is the point. A warmer baseline applies the heat island surcharge to a hotter city; and rising air-conditioning demand adds waste heat, which adds to the heat island — a reinforcing loop that also raises emissions.
- The consequence for public health. Rising hot-night counts, with a dense high-rise and ageing population, make heat stress a serious public-health issue — which is why the HKO issues heat warnings.
chunks.heading: 4. The urban heat island, and the interaction with the global trend

chunks.text:
- Sea surface temperature has risen, and marine heat stress affects South China Sea coral communities.
- Typhoon intensity. The number of tropical cyclones is not expected to increase, but the intensity of the most intense storms and their rainfall rates are expected to rise. With Hong Kong's proximity to the mainland coast, storm surge on an already-raised baseline is what matters.
- Ocean acidification affects the local marine ecosystem and fisheries. Arctic sea ice loss, though not a Hong Kong issue, is the clearest driver of the sea level rise Hong Kong experiences.
chunks.heading: 5. Other observed and projected trends

chunks.text:
Every one of these trends traces back to the same mechanism, and stating that lifts the answer above a list:

The global energy imbalance raises the baseline temperature and the baseline sea level; Hong Kong's own urban form adds a local heat surcharge on top of the temperature; and the city's drainage, coastal defence and public-health systems were designed against a baseline that no longer exists. So the city's exposure is increasing from two directions at once — which is why adaptation cannot be a one-off project but a continuous programme of upgrading.
chunks.heading: 6. The unifying statement

chunks.text:
- "Describe the observed trends in Hong Kong's climate": temperature (rate and period, plus the hot-night and very-hot-day indicators), rainfall (total and the pattern change), sea level (rate and period), and the urban heat island — each with a figure and a mechanism.
- "Explain why Hong Kong needs to keep upgrading drainage even though annual rainfall has not increased dramatically": the pattern shift — fewer, more intense events; hourly extremes up 29 to 38 per cent; and the concentration of risk in short periods.
- "Explain the implications of the rising sea level at Victoria Harbour": the baseline effect on storm surge, the Wanda and Hato comparison, land subsidence, and the projection of 0.63 to 1.07 m.
- "Discuss the implications of rising hot nights for Hong Kong": heat mortality and recovery, the ageing population, the urban heat island multiplier, and the health-system response.
- "Evaluate Hong Kong's climate vulnerability": exposure (dense coastal city, subsidence, high asset concentration) against adaptive capacity (wealth, technical capacity, an effective observatory and warning system) — and note that Hong Kong's vulnerability is about density and exposure rather than poverty.
chunks.heading: Answer structure

chunks.text:
- Quoting a rate without its period. "0.14 °C per decade" is the 1885–2025 figure; "0.35 °C per decade" is 1996–2025. Always say which.
- Saying 2025 was the hottest year on record. It was the sixth warmest.
- Confusing hot nights with very hot days — different thresholds, different health meanings, different counts.
- Missing the pattern point on rainfall. Total rainfall up 2.3 mm per year is the less important fact; the intensification of hourly extremes is the important one.
- Forgetting land subsidence as a local contributor to relative sea level rise.
- Ignoring the interaction between the global trend and the urban heat island, which is the local angle the examiner wants.
- Omitting the health dimension, which is why the hot-night indicator matters.
chunks.heading: Common marks lost

chunks.text:
1. Give Hong Kong's warming rate for 1885–2025 and for 1996–2025, and say why you would quote both.
2. Define hot night and very hot day, and give Hong Kong's averages for 1884–1913 and 1996–2025.
3. Explain why annual rainfall and flood risk can move in opposite directions.
4. Give the rate of sea level rise at Victoria Harbour and the period it applies to.
5. Compare Super Typhoon Wanda (1962) and Super Typhoon Hato (2017) and explain what the comparison shows.
6. Explain how Hong Kong is exposed from two directions at once.

docs.title: 7.23 Hong Kong's Policy Response (F6 Revision)
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP7/Concepts/7.23 Hong Kong's Policy Response (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why this is on the paper
This is the leaf where the module lands, and the examiner expects candidates to be specific: a candidate who says "Hong Kong promotes green development" scores nothing, while a candidate who names the Climate Action Plan 2050, its four strategies, the interim 2035 target and one instrument per strategy is quoting the material the examiner knows. The marks also reward the evaluation of Hong Kong's position — its structural constraints are the most interesting analytical content in the section.
chunks.heading: 7.23 Hong Kong's Policy Response (F6 Revision)

chunks.text:
- Carbon neutrality before 2050, and an interim target to reduce Hong Kong's carbon emissions by 50 per cent before 2035, compared with the 2005 level.
- Net-zero electricity generation, with the share of zero-carbon energy in the fuel mix for electricity generation to reach about 60 to 70 per cent by 2035.
- Alignment with national targets. China's "3060" dual-carbon goals — carbon peak before 2030, carbon neutrality before 2060 — frame Hong Kong's targets, and the Government has stated that its own align with them.
- The starting point. Total carbon emissions peaked in 2014 and have fallen since. In 2023 they were about 20 per cent below the 2005 level and a quarter below the 2014 peak.
chunks.heading: 1. The targets

chunks.text: The Hong Kong's Climate Action Plan 2050, promulgated in October 2021, is built on four decarbonisation strategies. Structure the whole section around them — that is the examiner's framework.
chunks.heading: 2. The four strategies of the Climate Action Plan 2050

chunks.text:
- Why electricity is the priority. Electricity generation accounted for about 61 per cent of Hong Kong's total carbon emissions in 2023, which in turn justifies making the fuel mix the centre of the plan.
- The fuel mix transition. Coal's share of electricity generation has fallen from about 50 per cent in 2015 to less than 20 per cent, while natural gas has risen above 50 per cent. Coal-fired generation is scheduled for phase-out by 2035.
- Nuclear. Hong Kong has imported nuclear electricity from the Daya Bay Nuclear Power Station since 1994, currently about a quarter of the fuel mix. The Government is discussing with the Mainland's National Energy Administration to increase zero-carbon supply, and has reserved land in Tseung Kwan O for receiving facilities.
- Renewables. Geography and building density constrain renewables — limited land, tall buildings, few open sites for wind or utility-scale solar, which in turn keeps the target modest: from less than 1 per cent of the fuel mix to 7.5 to 10 per cent by 2035, then 15 per cent subsequently. The Blueprint for Hong Kong's Energy Transition (2023) is the policy document.
chunks.heading: (a) Net-zero electricity generation

chunks.text:
- Buildings are the largest electricity consumers in a dense, high-rise city, so this is where electricity decarbonisation and demand-side decarbonisation meet.
- Regulatory framework. The Buildings Energy Efficiency Ordinance (BEEO) drives efficiency through codes of practice and mandatory energy audits for commercial buildings, administered through the Energy Audit Code. The target is to cut commercial building electricity consumption by 30 to 40 per cent from the 2005 level by 2035.
- Certification. The BEAM Plus system, introduced by the Hong Kong Green Building Council (HKGBC) in 2010, is Hong Kong's green-building assessment tool.
- Retrofit and behaviour. Energy audits create an information effect — a building that knows its consumption can target its waste — and support schemes help owners of older buildings, where savings potential is largest.
chunks.heading: (b) Energy saving and green buildings

chunks.text:
- Electrification, with the phase-out of petrol and diesel vehicles for new private cars by 2035 and the commitment to electrify most of the Government's fleet by then.
- Public transport, already a high share of journeys — the density and the rail network make modal shift available here in a way it is not in sprawling cities.
- The Blueprint also addresses electric vehicles, charging infrastructure, and green fuels for aviation and shipping.
- The complication. Electrifying vehicles only cuts emissions if the electricity is low-carbon — so transport and power policy are one policy.
chunks.heading: (c) Green transport

chunks.text:
- The Waste Blueprint for Hong Kong 2035 sets the vision of "zero waste landfilling" by 2035.
- The Integrated Waste Management Facilities: I·PARK1 on an artificial island off Shek Kwu Chau, Hong Kong's first modern waste-to-energy facility for municipal solid waste, with a design capacity of about 3,000 tonnes per day.
- Landfill gas from Hong Kong's landfills is captured and used to generate electricity.
- The abandoned instrument. The Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) Charging scheme, passed in 2021, was deferred in May 2024, and in September 2025 the Government confirmed it would not proceed, citing economic pressures and geopolitical uncertainty. It is retained as a reserve tool for use if voluntary measures fail.
chunks.heading: (d) Waste reduction

chunks.text:
The strengths:
- A clear, long-horizon framework with an interim 2035 milestone and four named strategies — more structure than many national plans have.
- Real implementation on power. The coal phase-out timetable and the fuel-mix shift are concrete, and with electricity at 61 per cent of emissions, progress there moves the city's total, which in turn makes it the clearest test of the targets.
- Institutional capability. A well-resourced, technically capable administration with a world-class meteorological observatory, a long planning horizon and the ability to fund large infrastructure.
chunks.heading: 3. Evaluating Hong Kong's position

chunks.text:
The structural constraints, which is the analytical heart of the section:
- Energy security and affordability. Hong Kong imports all its fossil fuel, so decarbonising power must not compromise the "safety, reliability, affordability and environmental performance" objectives. That is why the transition leans on imported nuclear power and interconnections rather than local renewables.
- Physical constraints on renewables. Few sites, high density, limited land mean the realistic renewable share is in single digits to low double digits. Hong Kong cannot follow Denmark's or California's model, so an answer that ignores this misses the case.
- Waste. Land scarcity makes disposal the binding constraint, so waste-to-energy, land reclamation and the shelved charging scheme are one story.
- Regional dependence. Electricity supply, waste disposal and much of the food and water depend on the Mainland and on international arrangements, so Hong Kong's climate policy is partly a regional policy, which in turn limits how much control Hong Kong has over its own emissions.
chunks.heading: 3. Evaluating Hong Kong's position

chunks.text: The honest verdict to write: Hong Kong's response is institutionally strong and its targets are clear, but they depend on external inputs — imported zero-carbon electricity, nuclear technology, and the Mainland's own energy transition — so Hong Kong's climate policy is one part of a larger regional project.
chunks.heading: 3. Evaluating Hong Kong's position

chunks.text:
- "Describe Hong Kong's response to climate change": the two targets and the four strategies of the Climate Action Plan 2050, with one specific instrument for each.
- "Evaluate the effectiveness of Hong Kong's climate policy": the targets and real progress on the fuel mix; then the constraints — land, energy security, waste, regional dependence; then the waste-charging failure, evidence that implementation is the weak point.
- "Explain why electricity generation is the priority in Hong Kong's climate policy": the 61 per cent share, and the knock-on to buildings and transport — decarbonising power addresses all three strategies at once.
- "Assess the problems of relying on nuclear power imported from the Mainland": it is genuinely zero-carbon, but it concentrates supply, depends on cross-boundary infrastructure (hence the reserved land in Tseung Kwan O), raises public acceptance questions, and does not remove the need to decarbonise at source.
- "Discuss why Hong Kong's renewable energy target is modest, and whether that is a problem": the physical constraints explain the target; but it means the bulk of the change must come from nuclear and imported zero-carbon electricity, which is where the risk sits.
- "Explain the significance of the abandonment of the waste charging scheme": it was a market instrument applying the polluter-pays principle; shelving it leaves only voluntary measures and the incinerators; and it shows the political-economy constraint.
chunks.heading: Answer structure

chunks.text:
- Vague policy language. Name the plan, the four strategies and the specific instruments.
- Forgetting the 2035 interim target — half of 2005 levels — which most candidates omit.
- Missing the four-strategy structure, which is the examiner's framework for the whole question.
- Not using the electricity share of emissions as the justification for the power-first strategy.
- Ignoring the constraints — land, energy security, import dependence. A question asking to "evaluate" wants them.
- Treating the waste charging scheme as still operating. It was deferred in 2024 and shelved in 2025.
- Overstating the renewable target. Hong Kong's target is 7.5 to 10 per cent of the fuel mix by 2035, rising to 15 per cent subsequently — not the headline figures of other places.
chunks.heading: Common marks lost

chunks.text:
1. State Hong Kong's two headline targets, with the baseline year for the interim target.
2. Name the four strategies of the Climate Action Plan 2050.
3. Why is electricity generation the priority in Hong Kong's climate policy? Give the share.
4. Explain why Hong Kong's realistic renewable share is modest, and name the target.
5. What has Hong Kong's waste policy achieved, and what was shelved in 2025?
6. Give two structural constraints on Hong Kong's climate policy and say which you think binds hardest.

docs.title: 7.3 Evidence of Global Warming (F6 Revision)
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP7/Concepts/7.3 Evidence of Global Warming (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why this is on the paper
"What evidence shows that the Earth is warming?" is the single most common CP7 opener, and it is usually worth the first few marks of a structured question. The examiner is not looking for a list of facts — they are looking for independent lines of evidence that converge on the same conclusion, because convergence is what makes a conclusion credible. A candidate who gives three pieces of evidence with no explanation of what each one measures scores half of what a candidate who says why each is independent gets.
chunks.heading: 7.3 Evidence of Global Warming (F6 Revision)

chunks.text:
Three tests, and they are worth stating explicitly in a top-band answer:

- Independence. The lines of evidence come from different systems — atmosphere, ocean, cryosphere, biosphere — and use different instruments. If they all relied on thermometers, a systematic thermometer error could explain them all. They do not.
- Convergence. Different proxies point the same way. That is what makes attribution to greenhouse gases credible.
- Consistency with theory. The evidence matches what the energy-balance mechanism predicts: more heat in the ocean, ice melting, sea level rising, more moisture in the atmosphere.
chunks.heading: 1. What makes evidence convincing

chunks.text:
- Global. Global mean surface temperature over 1850–1900 was about 1.1 °C lower than over 2011–2020 (IPCC AR6), with land warming faster than ocean — roughly +1.6 °C against +0.9 °C, because land has a lower heat capacity and no buffering mixing.
- Recent years. The World Meteorological Organization confirmed 2025 as the second or third-warmest year on record depending on the dataset, about 1.44 °C ± 0.13 °C above the 1850–1900 baseline. Copernicus ERA5 finds 2023–2025 was the first three-year period averaging above 1.5 °C; the WMO consolidated average is 1.48 °C, so quote the figure with its source.
- The mechanism behind the pattern. The warming is not a uniform, gentle drift. It shows year-to-year variability superimposed on a rising trend — El Niño and La Niña move individual years up or down, which in turn means a single cool year proves nothing. That is why the evidence question is phrased over a record, not a year.
chunks.heading: 2. Instrumental temperature records

chunks.text:
- Ocean heat content. The ocean has taken up more than 90 per cent of the excess heat in the climate system since 1970, and the rate of ocean warming since 1993 has more than doubled. This is why a warming Earth does not warm in a straight line in the air.
- Sea level. Global mean sea level rose about 20 cm between 1901 and 2018, and the rate has accelerated: roughly 1.3 mm per year over 1901–1971, 1.9 mm per year over 1971–2006, and 3.7 mm per year over 2006–2018 (IPCC AR6).
- Where the water comes from. Two contributions, and you should be able to give the split: thermal expansion of seawater as it warms (about half the total), and melting of glaciers and ice sheets (roughly two-fifths), with land water storage making up the rest. Naming only "ice melting" loses the warmer-ocean half.
- Recent level. By 2025, global mean sea level stood about 111 mm above the 1993 satellite baseline, a record high for the fourteenth consecutive year.
- Glaciers. In the 2025 hydrological year glaciers lost roughly 408 ± 132 gigatonnes of mass, equivalent to about 1.1 mm of sea level rise; six of the seven highest mass-loss years on record have occurred since 2019.
chunks.heading: 3. Ocean warming and sea level rise

chunks.text:
- Sea ice. Antarctic sea ice reached an annual minimum of about 1.98 million km² on 1 March 2025, tied for the second-lowest in the 47-year satellite record and roughly 860,000 km² below the 1981–2010 average.
- Why sea ice matters beyond itself. Open dark ocean absorbs far more solar energy than bright ice, so shrinking Arctic sea ice amplifies Arctic warming — evidence and mechanism in one.
- Permafrost. Warming thawing previously frozen ground releases both carbon dioxide and methane, which is both an impact and a feedback (see 7.2).
- Ice-sheet mass balance. Greenland and Antarctica are the two large ice sheets; both are losing mass, which is the single largest source of uncertainty in long-term sea level projection.
chunks.heading: 4. Cryosphere evidence

chunks.text:
Instrumental records only go back to the 1800s, which is far too short to separate a trend from natural variability. Ice cores solve this because air trapped in bubbles when the ice formed preserves a sample of the ancient atmosphere.

- What ice cores give. Direct measurements of atmospheric carbon dioxide and methane over roughly the last 800,000 years, alongside proxies for temperature.
- The key comparison. Modern concentrations of carbon dioxide are far above anything in that 800,000-year record. This is the single most powerful piece of evidence in the module, because it places today's warming in a geological context — it is not a natural fluctuation, it is departure from the range in which human civilisation evolved.
- Other proxies. Tree rings give annual temperature and precipitation over millennia; coral reefs record sea surface temperature and sea level; fossil records and ice cores together reconstruct past climate, and both show that climate has changed before — which is the honest qualification to add.
chunks.heading: 5. Ice cores and palaeoclimate: the long baseline

chunks.text:
- Species migration. Ranges shift poleward and upslope as the thermal envelope moves. The mechanism is that the climate to which a species is adapted moves; the species either follows at its own dispersal speed or declines.
- Phenology. Flowering, leafing, breeding and migration dates have shifted earlier, and the growing season lengthens in many mid- and high-latitude regions. Importantly, the signal is already visible in the fossil and pollen record too.
- Coral bleaching. Repeated bleaching events in the Great Barrier Reef and elsewhere show that marine heat stress is now exceeding the recovery capacity of reefs — a biological limit, not just a numerical one.
- Ocean acidification. Surface ocean pH has fallen by about 0.1 units since the industrial era, a roughly 26 per cent increase in hydrogen ion concentration, because the ocean absorbs around a quarter of anthropogenic carbon dioxide, which in turn makes it harder for shell-forming organisms to build carbonate skeletons — so the whole marine food web is affected.
chunks.heading: 6. Biological and phenological evidence

chunks.text:
A strong answer notes what the evidence does not prove on its own:

- The evidence shows warming; attributing it to human activity requires the fingerprint argument — that the pattern of warming (land warming faster than ocean, more heat in the ocean, night-time warming, reduced stratospheric cooling) matches the greenhouse gas fingerprint and not alternatives such as solar output or volcanic aerosols.
- The evidence shows change, not that every event is caused by climate change. Attribution of an individual storm or heatwave to climate change is a separate, more demanding statistical statement.
- 2025 was the second or third-warmest year, not the hottest. Precision protects you: 2024 was the record year, and the three-year average is what makes the point.
chunks.heading: 7. Reading the evidence properly

chunks.text:
- Describe / Explain: organise by evidence type, not by geography — (i) instrumental temperature, (ii) ocean warming and sea level, (iii) cryosphere, (iv) ice cores and palaeoclimate, (v) biological change. For each, say what it measures and what it shows.
- "How do we know it is human-caused?": name the fingerprint argument and the radiative forcing concept.
- "Evaluate the evidence": give the convergence argument, then the honest limits — short instrumental record, local variability, and the difficulty of attributing single events.
- Use data when it is supplied: describe the shape of the graph first (steady rise with variability; a step around a certain date), then quote one figure, then explain what caused the shape.
chunks.heading: Answer structure

chunks.text:
- A list of facts with no explanation of what each measures. "Sea level has risen" is a fact; "sea level has risen because warmer seawater expands and land ice has melted" is evidence with a mechanism.
- Quoting a year as the warmest. 2024 was the warmest; the three-year average is what makes the point.
- Forgetting the ice cores. Modern carbon dioxide concentrations are outside the range of the last 800,000 years — this is the strongest single argument in the module and many candidates omit it.
- Confusing "the evidence" with "the conclusion". The evidence shows warming; attribution to greenhouse gases is a further step with its own reasoning.
- Claiming every recent disaster was caused by climate change. Not supported, and it damages credibility in a "evaluate" question.
- Ignoring that climate has always changed. The natural baseline matters; the argument is about the rate and the cause of the current change.
chunks.heading: Common marks lost

chunks.text:
1. Give five independent lines of evidence for global warming, and say what each one measures.
2. Explain why ocean heat content is a more sensitive indicator of the energy imbalance than air temperature.
3. Give the two contributions to sea level rise and their approximate shares.
4. What does the ice-core record show about modern carbon dioxide concentrations, and why is that decisive?
5. Why must evidence be drawn from several independent systems rather than one?
6. A candidate says "the weather was unusually cool in 2015, so there is no global warming". Answer them in three sentences.

docs.title: 7.4 Weather, Climate & Scales (F6 Revision)
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP7/Concepts/7.4 Weather, Climate & Scales (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why this is on the paper
The weather/climate distinction is a low-mark, high-frequency trap: it appears in almost every CP7 structured question as the opening definition, and candidates lose marks by sliding from one to the other mid-answer. The scales question ("local, national, global") is what turns the definition into analysis — the examiner wants to know that the same global change looks different at each scale, and that the scale determines the evidence you would collect.
chunks.heading: 7.4 Weather, Climate & Scales (F6 Revision)

chunks.text:
| | Weather | Climate |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | The state of the atmosphere at a given place and moment — temperature, humidity, wind, rainfall, cloud, pressure | The statistical description of weather at a place over a long period, conventionally 30 years or more: means, variability, and the frequency of extremes |
| Timescale | Minutes to days; a few days in a forecast | Decades to millennia |
| Example | A cold, wet morning in October; a typhoon passing on a particular date | Hong Kong's October mean temperature, and the frequency of very hot days per year |

The single sentence to memorise: weather is what you observe today; climate is what the statistics of weather over 30 years look like. Climate is therefore not "the weather in the past" loosely — it is a summary built from weather, and it includes means and variability, not just averages.

Why the distinction is examinable: a candidate who writes "Hong Kong's climate has got hotter" after a single hot week has made a category error, and an examiner reading for evidence will look for the opposite error in a "global warming is a natural cycle" argument.
chunks.heading: 1. Weather versus climate: the definition

chunks.text:
The distinction that makes the whole topic work is between weather events (individual, noisy, and sometimes extreme) and the underlying statistical trend (slow, smooth, and directional).

- Variability comes from the coupled ocean–atmosphere system. El Niño and La Niña shift heat between the equatorial Pacific and the rest of the world, changing rainfall and temperature thousands of kilometres away. This is why an El Niño year can be hot in one hemisphere and cool in another.
- Natural cycles also operate on longer periods. Orbital (Milankovitch) changes in axial tilt, orbital shape and the distance from the Sun drove the glacial and interglacial cycles. These operate over tens of thousands of years — far too slowly to produce the warming of the last century.
- Therefore the evidence has to be a trend, not an event. This is the reasoning behind the "third-warmest year" precision in 7.3: individual years move up and down around a rising line, and only the line is diagnostic.
chunks.heading: 2. Natural variability versus the trend

chunks.text: At the local scale, climate is the expression of urban form and surface cover, not of global averages.
chunks.heading: 3. Local scale — microclimate and the urban heat island

chunks.text:
- Microclimate — the climate of a small area differing from the surrounding region. A hillside above the city, a park, a harbour, a high-rise podium: each has its own temperature, wind and humidity regime.
- Heat island effect (urban heat island) — urban areas are warmer than their surroundings. Mechanism in three steps: (i) urban materials such as concrete and asphalt have low albedo and high thermal mass, so they absorb shortwave radiation by day and release longwave radiation at night; (ii) impermeable surfaces and reduced vegetation suppress evapotranspiration, which in turn removes the latent-heat cooling that would otherwise occur; (iii) street canyons and dense building arrays reduce ventilation, and anthropogenic heat from air conditioning, vehicles and industry adds a further source.
- Which scale dominates which variable. At the local scale, land use and urban form dominate temperature. That is a crucial point: on a warm night, the difference between a park and a concrete plaza can exceed the difference between two cities over a century.
- Case anchor for Hong Kong: the contrast between the highly built-up Kowloon and the more open New Territories is the standard local illustration, and it links directly to CP4 (sustainable city) as well as CP7.
chunks.heading: 3. Local scale — microclimate and the urban heat island

chunks.text:
At the national scale, the picture is a country's own long-term statistics.

- Hong Kong as the worked example. The Hong Kong Observatory (HKO) has recorded at the Headquarters since 1884. The annual mean temperature rose at about 0.14 °C per decade over 1885–2025, and at a much faster 0.35 °C per decade over 1996–2025 — the acceleration is itself evidence. (See 7.22 for the full Hong Kong profile.)
- Why national scale is the most useful for policy. National trends are the scale at which governments legislate, and the scale at which the question "has this country warmed?" is meaningful for an economy, a health system and an infrastructure programme.
- National averages hide local exposure. A country's mean warming of 1 °C coexists with much larger changes in particular cities and particular sectors, so national-scale evidence is necessary but not sufficient.
chunks.heading: 4. National scale

chunks.text:
- Global mean surface temperature is the headline measure, and it is a mean, not a uniform change. Land warms faster than ocean; the Arctic warms faster still.
- Global aggregation smooths out variability, which is exactly what makes it the right scale for detecting a signal that is small relative to natural noise.
- Global figures are not local forecasts. A candidate who says "sea level will rise 20 cm everywhere by 2040" has over-read the global mean: local change differs because of ocean circulation, land subsidence or uplift, and sedimentation.
chunks.heading: 5. Global scale

chunks.text:
The best answers state explicitly that the scales are not independent layers; they are the same physical system observed at different resolutions.

1. Global forcing → regional signal. The global energy imbalance changes the global mean; regional climate change is that global change expressed through regional circulation, land-sea geometry and topography.
2. Regional signal → local extremes. A warmer atmosphere holds about 7 per cent more moisture per degree of warming, so the regional change in temperature determines the potential intensity of local extreme rainfall; local exposure and drainage then determine the damage.
3. Local modification → national statistics. Hong Kong's national warming rate is not a background condition it merely experiences — the city's own urban heat island, land reclamation and waste heat add to it, so national figures partly contain local decisions.

The sentence to earn the top band: climate change is a global-scale process whose impacts are filtered through regional climate systems and then modified at the local scale by urban form and land use — which is why mitigation must be global in scale while adaptation is local.
chunks.heading: 6. How the scales interact — the top-band move

chunks.text:
- Define and distinguish: give the two definitions, state the timescale (30-year convention), and make the contrast explicit in one sentence.
- "Explain how we know there is a climate trend rather than just variable weather": natural variability sources → the trend is visible over decades → cite an instrumental record or a multi-year average.
- "Discuss impacts at different scales": global (mean temperature, sea level) → regional (changing rainfall patterns, cyclone intensity, drought) → local (urban heat island, local flood risk), and say how each scale modifies the one above it.
- "Evaluate the view that a single extreme event proves or disproves global warming": reject both extremes, then explain the fingerprint and statistical-attribution approach.
chunks.heading: Answer structure

chunks.text:
- Sliding between weather and climate. "The climate has always changed" and "Hong Kong's climate was 33 °C yesterday" are both errors in opposite directions.
- Treating the 30-year average as the only content of climate. Climate also includes variability and extremes — the frequency of very hot days matters more to a city than the mean does.
- Confusing the urban heat island with global warming. The heat island is a local modification; it adds to, but is not caused by, the global trend. Confusing them is the single most common error in this section.
- Not naming the scale in a question that asks for local, national or global — label each point explicitly.
- Claiming global change is uniform. Global mean is an average; land, ocean and Arctic change at different rates.
- Ignoring natural variability. A candidate who never mentions El Niño or orbital cycles cannot explain why individual years move up and down.
chunks.heading: Common marks lost

chunks.text:
1. Define weather and climate, and state the timescale convention used for climate.
2. Why does a single cold year not disprove a warming trend, and what would?
3. Give the three mechanisms of the urban heat island.
4. Hong Kong's warming rate over 1885–2025 and over 1996–2025 — why do examiners quote both?
5. Explain how global warming produces a local flood event, in three steps.
6. A student says "the heat island effect proves that cities cause global warming". Correct them in two sentences.
