chunks.heading: Quick self-check

chunks.text:
Why this is on the paper
"What are the main greenhouse gases and their sources?" is a routine structured-question part, worth several easy marks that candidates routinely throw away by listing gases without their sources, or by confusing the strongest gas with the most abundant one. The examiner's version of the question usually asks you to rank or to link gas → source → policy, so build that three-step chain.
chunks.heading: 7.5 Greenhouse Gases (F6 Revision)

chunks.text:
A gas contributes to the greenhouse effect if it absorbs outgoing longwave radiation at wavelengths the surface emits, and then re-emits it. Two properties control how much warming a given amount of gas produces:

- Its strength of absorption — how much radiation it captures per molecule. Nitrous oxide is roughly two thousand times more potent than carbon dioxide per molecule.
- Its atmospheric lifetime — how long it stays in the atmosphere before it is removed. This is where the policy consequence lies: carbon dioxide persists for centuries, which in turn makes its effect effectively irreversible on human timescales, whereas methane lasts about a dozen years and therefore offers a faster lever if emissions are cut.

The distinction the examiner tests: potency per molecule and total effect on climate are different things. A gas can be potent but small in quantity (nitrous oxide), or abundant but less potent per molecule (carbon dioxide). Methane is intermediate — less abundant than carbon dioxide, more potent per molecule, shorter-lived.
chunks.heading: 1. What makes a gas a greenhouse gas

chunks.text:
| Gas | Principal sources | Approximate atmospheric lifetime | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| Carbon dioxide (CO₂) | Burning coal, oil and natural gas; cement production; deforestation and land-use change | Centuries to millennia — the bulk of a pulse decays over hundreds of years | The largest contributor to the enhanced greenhouse effect by total human emissions; controls the long-term outcome |
| Methane (CH₄) | Livestock digestion and manure; rice paddies; landfill gas; oil and gas leaks; termites in some land-use change | Roughly 12 years | Short-lived, so cuts deliver rapid climate benefit; also a far more powerful greenhouse gas than CO₂ per molecule |
| Nitrous oxide (N₂O) | Nitrogen fertilisers; industrial processes; burning fossil fuels and biomass | About a century | Potent and persistent; also destroys ozone in the stratosphere |
| Ozone (O₃) | Photochemical reaction of nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds; also natural stratospheric ozone | Days in the troposphere (short-lived, a pollutant) | A pollutant near the surface, a different substance from the protective stratospheric ozone |
| Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and HFCs | Refrigeration, air conditioning, foam production, aerosol propellants | Centuries for CFCs; years to decades for many HFCs | Extremely potent; the main family targeted by the Montreal Protocol, which is why their growth has slowed |
| Water vapour (H₂O) | Evaporation from oceans, lakes, soils and vegetation | Days to weeks | The largest contributor to the natural greenhouse effect, but a feedback, not a forcing — it amplifies warming rather than causing it |
chunks.heading: 2. The main gases: source, lifetime and role

chunks.text: The water-vapour point is worth a mark on its own. It is the most abundant greenhouse gas, but you cannot mitigate it directly; you mitigate the temperature change that increases it. That makes it the classic example of a feedback, and it links straight back to the feedback section in 7.2.
chunks.heading: 2. The main gases: source, lifetime and role

chunks.text:
Longevity is not just trivia — it determines which lever a government should pull.

- Carbon dioxide's century-plus lifetime means emissions already made are effectively committed. Cutting emissions today still prevents warming that would have occurred later, but the planet does not return to its previous temperature.
- Methane's roughly 12-year lifetime means cutting methane emissions produces a measurable climate response within a decade. This is why methane is central to the near-term ambition of agreements such as the Paris Agreement.
- CFCs and HFCs, being both potent and long-lived, deliver the best ratio of climate benefit per unit of political effort, and they were the first family of gases to be successfully regulated — through the Montreal Protocol, which is the clearest precedent in the whole module of a global treaty that actually worked.
chunks.heading: 3. The policy meaning of lifetime

chunks.text:
Examiners often want the gases linked to sectors, because that is where policy bites.

| Sector | Principal gases | Mechanism of the link |
|---|---|---|
| Power generation | CO₂, with some N₂O and CH₄ | Burning fossil fuel releases the carbon stored in the fuel as CO₂ |
| Transport | CO₂, plus N₂O from catalytic converters and CH₄ from fuel leaks | Combustion of petrol and diesel; also from upstream production of the fuel |
| Industry | CO₂, N₂O, HFCs, PFCs | Process emissions (cement, steel, aluminium, chemicals) plus combustion; HFCs come from refrigerant leakage, not from burning anything |
| Agriculture and land use | CH₄, N₂O, CO₂ | Livestock digestion, manure, rice cultivation, fertiliser use; and deforestation releasing both stored carbon and reducing the uptake of CO₂ by growing vegetation |
| Waste | CH₄ | Anaerobic decomposition of organic waste in landfill, producing landfill gas |
| Cooling and refrigeration | HFCs, CFCs | Leakage of refrigerant gases, which are designed to be chemically stable and to trap heat |
| Buildings | Indirect CO₂ | Emissions are booked to the electricity generation that powers them — which is why, in Hong Kong, buildings and power together dominate the city's carbon footprint |
chunks.heading: 4. Where the emissions come from: the sector view

chunks.text:
- Forcing — a change in the radiative balance directly caused by human activity. Adding CO₂, methane or nitrous oxide is forcing.
- Feedback — a response to that forcing that amplifies or dampens it. Water vapour, ice-albedo, permafrost carbon and fire are all feedbacks.

Why this matters for the mitigation argument: you cannot mitigate a feedback directly, because feedbacks respond to the temperature that forcing has already produced. Mitigation has to target the forcings — and that is why the Paris Agreement and national targets are written in terms of emissions of specific gases rather than of temperature.
chunks.heading: 5. The distinction that carries the marks: forcing versus feedback

chunks.text:
- Identify and describe: name the gases; for each give source, lifetime and relative importance; state which is the largest contributor by total human emissions (CO₂).
- Explain how a gas causes warming: absorb outgoing longwave → re-emit in all directions → more energy retained → warming. Say which step changes with more of the gas.
- "Explain why methane matters despite being less abundant than CO₂": potency per molecule plus the shorter lifetime that makes it a fast lever for near-term temperature control.
- "Discuss why controlling greenhouse gases is difficult": long lifetimes, diffuse sources (agriculture, transport, household waste), and the fact that some gases are inputs to other economic activity rather than by-products.
- "Evaluate the use of CFCs as a precedent": the Montreal Protocol worked because the substitute was available, the industry cooperated, and the gas was visible and identifiable in products — contrast that with CO₂, which is invisible and embedded in the whole economy.
chunks.heading: Answer structure

chunks.text:
- Listing gases without sources. Each gas needs a source and a mechanism.
- Treating water vapour as a cause rather than a feedback. It is not directly mitigable.
- Confusing ground-level ozone with the ozone layer. Ground-level ozone is a pollutant formed by vehicle and industry emissions; stratospheric ozone is protective.
- Saying methane is "the most harmful gas". It is more potent per molecule; CO₂ dominates the total effect. Precision here is directly rewarded.
- Confusing potency with abundance when asked to rank gases by contribution to warming.
- Omitting lifetime when the question asks about the difficulty of mitigation — persistence is the mechanism that makes CO₂ effectively irreversible.
- Forgetting that refrigerant gases (HFCs) come from leaks, not combustion, so "reduce fossil fuel use" does not address them.
chunks.heading: Common marks lost

chunks.text:
1. Name the four main greenhouse gases and give one source for each.
2. Why is water vapour classified as a feedback rather than a forcing?
3. Give the two reasons methane is more attractive than CO₂ as a near-term target.
4. Why is the Montreal Protocol often cited as the strongest precedent for climate treaty success?
5. Which Hong Kong sectors would you expect to carry the largest emissions, and through which gases?
6. Explain in two sentences why the persistence of CO₂ makes the problem "unavoidable but not hopeless".

Source note: CP7_Global_Warming_Detailed_Notes · current cases CP7 Update Cases 2025-2026 · index DSE_SUMMARY · previous: 7.4 Weather, Climate & Scales (F6 Revision) · next: 7.6 Human Activities (F6 Revision)
chunks.heading: Quick self-check

chunks.text:
Why this is on the paper
"What human activities cause global warming?" is the other half of the causes question, and the examiner wants activity → substance released → mechanism → effect, not a shopping list. The high-value move is explaining land-use change as well as fossil fuels, because candidates who name only combustion have missed a whole pathway — and deforestation has a second-order effect that reinforces the first.
chunks.heading: 7.6 Human Activities (F6 Revision)

chunks.text:
Human activity warms the planet through two broad routes, and they work differently:

- Pathway A — emission. Burning something releases gases that were stored in it. This adds to atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations.
- Pathway B — removal. Clearing or degrading land removes the vegetation and soils that were absorbing gases. This reduces the sinks that would otherwise have taken up emissions, and in the case of deforestation also releases stored carbon.

Both pathways reduce the net amount of greenhouse gas in the atmosphere. A full answer needs both.
chunks.heading: 1. The two great pathways

chunks.text:
- What it does. Coal, oil and natural gas are carbon-bearing compounds that took millions of years to form. Burning them oxidises the carbon and releases it as CO₂, adding to the atmospheric concentration directly.
- Where it happens. Electricity generation (the largest single source globally), transport (road, aviation and shipping), industry and manufacturing, and heating in buildings.
- Why it dominates the policy debate. Fossil fuels are not just an energy source; they are the foundation of industrial economies, transport systems and food production. Every one of those sectors was built on them, so decarbonising requires rebuilding infrastructure, not swapping a light bulb.
- Coal versus oil versus gas. Coal is the most carbon-intensive per unit of energy; gas emits roughly half as much CO₂ as coal and less than oil, which is why it is sometimes presented as a "transition fuel" — though it is still a fossil fuel, and methane leakage erodes the advantage, which in turn limits how much it can carry the transition.
- The Hong Kong illustration. Around 60 per cent of Hong Kong's carbon emissions come from electricity generation, and buildings consume most of that electricity. So in Hong Kong, decarbonising power and decarbonising buildings are close to the same policy problem.
chunks.heading: 2. Fossil fuel combustion

chunks.text:
- The direct effect. Clearing forest for agriculture, pasture, mining or infrastructure removes vegetation that was photosynthesising and absorbing CO₂, and in most cases releases the carbon stored in the tree biomass and the soil.
- The second-order effect, the mark-winning one. A forest is not just a carbon store; it is part of a hydrological cycle. Large tropical forest generates rainfall recycled across the region. Deforestation reduces that recycling, so the region becomes drier, raising fire risk, which releases more carbon, causing further drying — a compounding loop.
- The fire link. Indonesia and the Congo Basin have repeatedly seen major peat fires. Peat can hold several times more carbon per hectare than tropical forest, and burning it takes decades to regrow. The 2025 Borneo fires during the developing super El Niño are the current illustration.
- The offset point. Emissions from land-use change are sometimes counted net of what would have happened anyway — the "counterfactual" argument. Legitimate accounting, but one of the most contested areas of climate science, because the counterfactual is unobservable. Examiners like this as a discussion point.
chunks.heading: 3. Land-use change and deforestation

chunks.text:
- Methane from livestock. Ruminant digestion and manure management release CH₄, which is potent and short-lived.
- Methane from rice. Anaerobic flooded paddy soils produce CH₄.
- Nitrous oxide from fertiliser. Nitrogen fertilisers applied to soils produce N₂O, both directly and through microbial processes; over-application also pollutes water and reduces soil carbon.
- The second-order effect: land pressure. As diets in middle-income populations shift toward more meat and dairy, demand for feed and pasture increases, expanding the agricultural frontier, which drives deforestation — a strong essay link.
- Food waste. About a third of food produced globally is lost or wasted, and that unused food embodied the emissions of its production, plus refrigeration and transport.
chunks.heading: 4. Agriculture and food systems

chunks.text:
- Industrial process emissions. Cement, steel, aluminium and chemicals release CO₂ from the chemistry itself, not only from burning fuel — so these cannot be solved by switching to clean electricity alone.
- Refrigerants. Leakage of HFCs from air conditioning and refrigeration is a high-potency, high-volume emission source, and it is rising as cooling demand rises with warming. That is an example of a feedback in the policy system: warming drives up cooling, which drives up emissions.
- Buildings. Nearly 40 per cent of global energy-related emissions come from the buildings sector, largely through heating, cooling, lighting and appliances; buildings are also a major sink for HFC leakage.
- Transport. Road transport dominates. Electric vehicles shift emissions from the tailpipe to the power station, which is a real reduction only if the electricity is low-carbon — the same electricity decarbonisation drives both transport and building benefits.
chunks.heading: 5. Industry, buildings and urban form

chunks.text:
- Landfill methane. Anaerobic decomposition of organic waste produces methane and CO₂. Hong Kong's Integrated Waste Management Facilities (I·PARK1 at Shek Kwu Chau, and I·PARK2 planned at Tsang Tsui, Tuen Mun) treat municipal solid waste by advanced incineration with energy recovery — which diverts waste from landfill and generates electricity.
- The honest evaluation. Incineration is not carbon-neutral: it reduces landfill methane and recovers energy, but the CO₂ in the plastics fraction is still released unless the facility runs on low-carbon electricity. Waste-to-energy therefore belongs in a hierarchy of reduce, reuse, recycle, recover energy, landfill — it is not a licence to keep generating waste.
- The policy lever that was shelved. Hong Kong's Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) Charging scheme was legislated in 2021, deferred in May 2024, and in September 2025 confirmed it would not proceed, relying instead on voluntary recycling and the waste-to-energy facilities. A superb exam case: a market instrument abandoned for political reasons.
- The general principle: waste reduction attacks the problem at source; incineration manages the residue. Only the first reduces total emissions.
chunks.heading: 6. The waste pathway, and why it is not trivial

chunks.text:
When a question asks you to weigh the causes, the strong answer makes three moves:

1. The fingerprint argument. The observed pattern of warming — land warming faster than ocean, more heat stored in the ocean, night-time temperatures rising faster than daytime, and the stratosphere cooling — matches the fingerprint of greenhouse gas forcing, not of solar variability or volcanic aerosols.
2. The timing argument. Warming accelerated sharply in the second half of the twentieth century, coinciding with the post-war expansion of fossil fuel use, not with any change in solar output.
3. The energy-balance argument. Since the incoming solar term is essentially fixed on human timescales, an increase in retained energy must come from changes in the outgoing term, and the only substantial mechanism available on this timescale is greenhouse gas concentration.
chunks.heading: 7. Evaluating "how important is human activity?"

chunks.text:
- Identify and explain: activity → gas released → mechanism (more longwave absorbed) → effect on the energy balance. Do this for at least fossil fuels, land-use change and agriculture.
- "Assess the relative importance of fossil fuel combustion and deforestation": compare scale, reversibility and feasibility of reversal, and note the compounding land–fire–dryness loop.
- "Explain how urbanisation contributes to climate change": buildings, transport, waste, loss of vegetation, and the heat island feedback — remembering that urbanisation also removes a carbon sink.
- "Evaluate waste-to-energy as a solution": diverts from landfill, recovers energy, but does not reduce the carbon in plastics; must sit inside a hierarchy that starts with reduction.
- "To what extent is human activity the only cause?": present the natural causes, then the fingerprint, timing and energy-balance arguments, then the honest statement that natural variability sets the weather but the trend is human.
chunks.heading: Answer structure

chunks.text:
- Naming activities without the mechanism. "Burning fossil fuels causes global warming" is the question restated.
- Ignoring land-use change, or mentioning it only as "deforestation releases CO₂" without the regional drying and fire loop.
- Treating all sectors as equally large. Electricity generation and industry dominate globally; the candidate who lists "transport" and "farming" first has the scale wrong.
- Saying electric vehicles solve transport emissions without qualifying that they depend on the electricity mix.
- Calling waste-to-energy a clean solution. It manages waste; it does not reduce total carbon.
- Forgetting the counterfactual problem in land-use accounting — it is a genuine scientific debate and a good evaluation point.
- Confusing "human activity" with "pollution" or "industry" — the biggest anthropogenic source is the burning of energy, which is what an advanced economy does every day.
chunks.heading: Common marks lost

chunks.text:
1. Explain how deforestation can cause regional rainfall to decline, and what follows from that.
2. Name the four fossil-fuel combustion sectors and rank them by global share.
3. Why are cement and steel emissions not solved by switching to renewable electricity?
4. Explain the mechanism by which warming increases cooling demand and therefore emissions.
5. Give three reasons the Hong Kong waste-charging scheme was shelved, and say which policy instrument it was.
6. State the three arguments that attribute the observed warming to human activity, and say which is most robust.

docs.path: DSE Geography/CP7/Concepts/7.7 Natural vs Human Causes (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why this is on the paper
This is the module's flagship evaluate question. The examiner is not looking for "human causes are more important because they are worse" — they are looking for you to build the case properly: state the natural causes with their mechanism, state the human case with its evidence, and then weigh them. The strongest answers also explain why the question is subtler than it looks, because the natural and human causes operate on different timescales and in different parts of the system.
chunks.heading: 7.7 Natural vs Human Causes (F6 Revision)

chunks.text:
- Volcanic eruptions. Eruptions inject sulphate aerosols into the stratosphere, which reflect incoming shortwave radiation and cool the planet for a year or two. The mechanism is the opposite of the greenhouse effect: they act on the incoming term, not the outgoing term. Examples: Mount Pinatubo in 1991, and Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai in 2022, which had a measurable cooling effect in the year after the eruption.
- Solar variability. Changes in solar output vary on multi-decadal cycles and are small — around 0.1 per cent over the past few decades, against a warming of more than 1 °C. The magnitude alone rules it out as the main driver.
- Orbital (Milankovitch) cycles. Changes in axial tilt, orbital eccentricity and the tilt of the ecliptic alter the seasonal and latitudinal distribution of sunlight. They drive the ice ages — but over tens of thousands of years, which is why they cannot produce warming of the last century.
- Natural variability (El Niño / La Niña). These redistribute heat between the equatorial Pacific and the rest of the system, producing large year-to-year and multi-year swings in regional temperature and rainfall — but they produce no long-term trend, because the system returns to its prior state, which in turn makes them incapable of explaining a sustained rise.
- Natural vegetation and wildfire. Wildfires release carbon, but the regrowth that follows reabsorbs much of it, so the long-run balance is roughly neutral.
chunks.heading: 1. The natural causes, with mechanisms

chunks.text: What all the natural causes have in common: they act either on the incoming term or by redistributing energy in time and place. None of them adds heat to the system on a sustained basis, except the very long orbital ones which operate far too slowly.
chunks.heading: 1. The natural causes, with mechanisms

chunks.text:
- The mechanism is different in kind. Human activity adds greenhouse gases, which reduce the outgoing term, so the system must store the surplus.
- The evidence base: see 7.7's three arguments — fingerprint, timing, energy balance.
- The scale: human emissions are now large enough to dominate the natural forcing entirely. The current anthropogenic radiative forcing is roughly 2.7 to 3.0 W m⁻² (IPCC AR6 estimate), which is larger than the combined forcing from all natural sources in the preceding two thousand years.
chunks.heading: 2. The human case

chunks.text:
This is the top-band material. Three qualifications make the answer sophisticated:

1. Natural variability still controls the weather, including extremes. A heatwave in Europe in 2025 is a product of blocking high-pressure systems and a warmer baseline. Climate change does not "cause" individual events; it changes the probability distribution in which they occur — it makes them more frequent and more intense. So the natural and human causes are not rivals; they act on different stages of the same chain.
2. Natural systems modulate the human signal. Volcanic aerosols can mask warming for a year or two — which is exactly why the trend must be read over decades, not years.
3. The "natural" is not a moral category. Some natural causes are triggered by human activity: wildfire in a deforested, drained peatland is a human-modified system; the drying of a region that drives Amazon die-back is partly caused by deforestation and warming elsewhere. Attribution of a specific event can therefore involve both.
chunks.heading: 3. The case that the debate is subtler than it looks

chunks.text:
This is the part of the question that rewards a genuine evaluative judgement.

The case that the trend is irreversible (or very nearly so):

- Ocean inertia. The ocean has taken up more than 90 per cent of the excess heat. Even if emissions fell to net zero tomorrow, the surface would continue warming for decades as the ocean mixed that heat upward, and some of it would never leave the ocean.
- CO₂ persistence. A large fraction of emitted CO₂ is removed only over centuries to millennia. Atmospheric concentration would keep rising for decades after emissions stopped.
- Ice-sheet commitment. Once ice sheets begin to lose mass, the process continues for centuries to millennia even if temperature stabilises, because of glacial response times.
- Irreversibility in ecosystems. Species that have migrated or gone extinct do not return; coral reef damage at scale takes decades to centuries to recover, if it recovers at all.

The case that it is not irreversible:
chunks.heading: 4. The irreversible-trend debate

chunks.text:
- Nothing in physics requires continued warming. If net emissions fall to zero, the energy balance is restored and the temperature stabilises at a higher level — but it does not continue rising indefinitely. This is a real and important distinction: the trend in emissions versus the trend in temperature versus the irreversibility of the impacts.
- Adaptation and remediation exist. Afforestation and carbon capture remove carbon from the atmosphere; sea walls, zoning and early-warning systems reduce damage. The Netherlands, Tuvalu and Bangladesh all show adaptation working at scale.
- The magnitude of the irreversible part is policy-dependent. How much warming occurs in the first place determines how much must be adapted to. Mitigation is therefore the policy that determines the scale of the adaptation problem — which is why mitigation and adaptation are not alternatives but complements.
- Tipping points are a separate question from irreversibility. Some tipping points (such as the collapse of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation or the die-back of the Amazon) are genuinely self-reinforcing once crossed. Whether and when they are crossed depends on how much warming occurs — so mitigation still reduces the probability.
chunks.heading: 4. The irreversible-trend debate

chunks.text: The judgement the examiner wants: the trend in global temperature is likely to continue for decades because of ocean inertia and the persistence of CO₂, but it is not physically inevitable to continue indefinitely; and the impacts already locked in — species loss, sea level, ice-sheet mass loss — are effectively irreversible on any human planning horizon. Therefore the correct policy conclusion is not "adapt or mitigate" but "mitigate hard enough to bound the adaptation problem, and adapt to what is already committed."
chunks.heading: 4. The irreversible-trend debate

chunks.text:
- "Evaluate the view that global warming is caused entirely by human activity": (i) state the natural causes with mechanism; (ii) state the human cause with mechanism; (iii) the three arguments (fingerprint, timing, energy balance, plus magnitude of forcing); (iv) the qualification that natural variability governs individual events; (v) verdict — the recent warming is human-caused, but individual events and the underlying variability remain natural.
- "Discuss the view that the trend is irreversible": separate the three meanings of irreversible — temperature trend, atmospheric CO₂, and impacts; give the ocean-inertia and persistence arguments; then the counter-arguments (physics does not require continued warming; adaptation works; mitigation determines the scale of the commitment); then a verdict.
- "To what extent has natural variability been overshadowed by human-induced change?": use the probability-distribution argument — you do not need to attribute a single event to explain a shift in the odds.
chunks.heading: Answer structure

chunks.text:
- Only listing natural causes — the candidate who names volcanoes and orbital cycles and stops is in the bottom band, because they never address the human case.
- Only listing human causes — mid-band at best; the "evaluate" command requires both sides.
- Confusing natural variability with natural forcing. El Niño does not add heat to the system; it moves it. Say so.
- "We cannot say for certain that humans caused it." The scientific attribution is the attribution to human influence with quantified confidence. Overstating the uncertainty is the mark-loser here.
- Conflating three different irreversibilities — this is the single biggest analytical trap in the topic. Separate them explicitly.
- Treating "irreversible" as "unstoppable", and therefore concluding that mitigation is pointless. The correct conclusion is that mitigation determines the scale of what must be adapted to.
- Missing the probability-distribution point — the best single sentence in the whole debate is "climate change does not cause individual events; it changes how likely they are."
chunks.heading: Common marks lost

chunks.text:
1. Give four natural causes of climate change and state the timescale of each.
2. Why can volcanic eruptions not explain warming since 1950?
3. State the three arguments that attribute the observed warming to human influence.
4. Explain the fingerprint argument in three sentences, and name three features of it.
5. Separate "irreversible warming", "irreversible CO₂" and "irreversible impacts" — why must a good answer treat them differently?
6. Explain why the ocean makes the temperature trend lag the emissions trend.

docs.title: 7.8 Garbage Burning & Human Activities (F6 Revision)
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP7/Concepts/7.8 Garbage Burning & Human Activities (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why this is on the paper
"Garbage burning" is one of the few places where the syllabus names a specific, everyday human activity rather than a sector. That makes it a favourite for structured questions and local fieldwork-flavoured prompts, and it bridges CP7's causes and CP4's waste problems. The examiner wants the mechanism of a small, direct, local emission source, and — crucially — where the answer is not "stop burning" but a hierarchy.
chunks.heading: 7.8 Garbage Burning & Human Activities (F6 Revision)

chunks.text:
The composition of the smoke depends on what is burned, and the mechanism follows from that:

- Carbon dioxide — from the carbon in plastics, paper, textiles and organic waste. This is the dominant long-lived contribution, entering the same energy-balance mechanism as any other CO₂ source.
- Water vapour and, in incomplete combustion, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and fine particulates — the co-pollutants of open burning.
- Dioxins and furans — from burning chlorinated plastics in poor conditions; persistent, carcinogenic and bioaccumulative, contaminating soil, water and the food chain downwind. This is why open burning is regulated as a public-health measure as much as a climate one.
- Methane and landfill gas — the avoided emission: burning waste that would otherwise decompose anaerobically in landfill prevents methane, a far more powerful greenhouse gas per molecule than CO₂.
- Black carbon — warms by absorbing sunlight; near the ground its effect is warming.

The key analytical point: garbage burning is a small contributor to global greenhouse gas emissions but a large and locally intense one. At the neighbourhood scale, the health and particulate damage dominates the climate argument; at the global scale it is minor.
chunks.heading: 1. What burning garbage actually emits

chunks.text:
Examiners like candidates to explain the cause of the practice, because the cause determines the policy:

1. No or unaffordable collection. Where collection is absent, irregular or costly, burning is the cheapest way to dispose of waste. The behaviour is rational for the household.
2. No landfill or transfer station within reach. Distance is decisive: waste that would be carried a short way is burned instead.
3. Poverty and informal livelihoods. Waste pickers burn the uncollected fraction to recover what has value; open burning of recyclables is common where the price of recovered material is low.
4. Open burning as a livelihood. The char and ash from burning plastic are sometimes sold for use in bricks or as fuel, so the practice has an economic reason a ban alone does not remove.
5. No visible alternative. Where recycling infrastructure does not exist, the "reduce and recycle" message has no physical mechanism behind it.

The consequence chain: poor collection → open burning → CO₂, particulates and dioxins → warming plus direct health damage in the communities that burn. That single chain answers both the "cause" and the "impact" halves of a question.
chunks.heading: 2. Why people burn waste — the mechanism behind the behaviour

chunks.text:
- Open burning of agricultural residue is a significant global source of black carbon, particularly in South and Southeast Asia, and also in sub-Saharan Africa and South America.
- Peat fires in Indonesia and the Congo Basin are a related phenomenon: drainage of peatland for plantations exposes peat that smoulders for years, releasing very large quantities of CO₂ and methane.
- The 2025 event. During the developing super El Niño, extensive fires burned in Kalimantan and in Java — where the fires sat on cropland rather than peat. That contrast proves the peatland mechanism: the same weather produces far more carbon loss on drained peat than on mineral soil.
- The Congo Basin is the second great peat and forest-fire region, its fires strongly linked to deforestation for commercial agriculture.
chunks.heading: 3. The global picture: open burning in the tropics

chunks.text:
A question asking how to reduce the emissions from waste has a structured answer, and the order is the mark:

| Stage | Action | Climate effect | Practical difficulty |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Reduce | Prevent waste; reuse and repair; avoid single-use items | The only stage that removes the emissions entirely | Needs behaviour change and product redesign |
| 2. Recycle | Separate and reprocess materials | Avoids both the CO₂ of incineration and the methane of landfill, and keeps the material's embedded value | Needs collection, sorting and markets |
| 3. Recover energy | Waste-to-energy incineration | Diverts from landfill and recovers energy, but still releases the CO₂ in the plastics fraction | Capital cost; emissions depend on the electricity mix |
| 4. Landfill | Engineered, gas-captured landfill | The residual; methane can be captured and flared, but the carbon is still released | Least attractive; site-limited |

Why the order matters for the climate: only reduction at source lowers total carbon. Recycling avoids emissions; waste-to-energy relocates them from methane to CO₂; landfill, even with gas capture, is the end of the chain. A candidate who writes "incinerate everything" has skipped the top two rows.
chunks.heading: 4. The solution hierarchy — the marking point

chunks.text: Hong Kong makes this concrete and is the natural local anchor:
chunks.heading: 5. The Hong Kong case

chunks.text:
- Municipal solid waste is generated by a city of seven-plus million people with high consumption, and land is scarce, so the disposal options are narrow.
- The Waste Blueprint for Hong Kong 2035 sets the vision of "zero waste landfilling" by 2035, pursued through waste reduction at source, recycling, and adequate waste-to-energy capacity.
- I·PARK1, on an artificial island off Shek Kwu Chau, is Hong Kong's first modern waste-to-energy facility for municipal solid waste, with a design capacity of about 3,000 tonnes per day; trial operation began at the end of 2025. I·PARK2 is being built at Tsang Tsui, Tuen Mun.
- The gap between the two strategies is the case. The Municipal Solid Waste Charging scheme, legislated in 2021, was deferred in May 2024 and in September 2025 the Government confirmed it would not proceed. This shows the tension between a market instrument (a price on disposal) and a service instrument (an alternative).
- Waste charging applies the "polluter pays" principle and price elasticity: a charge on disposal raises the cost of throwing things away, shifting behaviour towards reduction and recycling — but only where an alternative system exists, which is why the deferral mattered.
- The landfill-gas connection: gas from Hong Kong's landfills is captured and used to generate electricity, converting a methane source into useful energy.
chunks.heading: 5. The Hong Kong case

chunks.text:
- For incineration: it removes volume, produces energy, avoids land occupation, and diverts waste that would otherwise generate methane; it is more publicly acceptable than landfill, reducing illegal dumping and open burning.
- Against incineration: it is expensive and slow to build; it locks a city into capacity it may not need if waste reduction succeeds; it does not reduce total carbon; it produces fly ash needing hazardous-waste handling; and it is politically unpopular.
- Against a waste charge: it is regressive unless compensated, it needs an adequate public service to be accepted, and it can be shelved when the economy is weak — again, Hong Kong's experience.
chunks.heading: 6. Evaluating a local scheme

chunks.text:
- Explain how garbage burning contributes to global warming: combustion releases CO₂ from the carbon in the waste → adds to greenhouse gas concentrations → more longwave absorbed → warming. Add that the local damage (particulates, dioxins) is a health issue rather than a climate issue.
- "Explain why people burn garbage": collection absent or costly → distance and poverty → burning as the cheapest option → the policy implication that the fix is a collection and recycling system.
- "Discuss ways to reduce the greenhouse effect of waste": give the four-stage hierarchy in order, explain why each stage works, and state which alone reduces total carbon.
- "Evaluate the waste-to-energy strategy in Hong Kong": the advantages, the carbon caveat, the lock-in concern, the ash issue and the political problem — with the shelving of the waste charging scheme as evidence.
chunks.heading: Answer structure

chunks.text:
- Saying burning garbage "pollutes the environment" without naming the gas and the mechanism.
- Missing the methane trade-off. Open burning avoids landfill methane; a candidate who only lists negatives has not evaluated.
- Confusing open burning with the flue-gas emissions of a modern incinerator — a properly designed facility with flue-gas treatment is a different proposition from an open fire.
- Giving "burn less rubbish" as a solution — that is the conclusion, not the mechanism.
- Failing to order the waste hierarchy, or putting incineration first.
- Ignoring the Hong Kong politics — the deferral and then shelving of the waste charging scheme is the strongest local material in the topic, and shows that climate policy has to survive elections.
chunks.heading: Common marks lost

chunks.text:
1. Name the main gases emitted by open waste burning and the health pollutant of greatest concern.
2. Explain, using the peat-versus-cropland contrast, why the same fire season produces more carbon loss in one place than another.
3. Why does burning waste avoid one greenhouse gas and produce another?
4. Put the four stages of the waste hierarchy in order and say which reduces total carbon.
5. Give two advantages and two disadvantages of Hong Kong's waste-to-energy strategy, using the I·PARK1 case.
6. Why did the Hong Kong Government shelve the waste charging scheme, and what does that tell you about policy instruments?

Source note: CP7_Global_Warming_Detailed_Notes · current cases CP7 Update Cases 2025-2026 · index DSE_SUMMARY · previous: 7.7 Natural vs Human Causes (F6 Revision) · next: 7.9 Physical Impacts (F6 Revision)
chunks.heading: Quick self-check

chunks.text:
Why this is on the paper
The physical/social split is the spine of the impacts question, and examiners mark it rigidly: a candidate who mixes environmental and social consequences in one list scores as though they have answered only half. In the physical half, the examiner rewards mechanism chains with energy-balance roots — sea level rise is not "ice melts" but "warming causes expansion and melting, and both add volume". Name the process, then the consequence, then who it hits.
chunks.heading: 7.9 Physical Impacts (F6 Revision)

chunks.text:
Two independent contributions, and a candidate who names only one has half the answer:

1. Thermal expansion. Water expands when heated, so the ocean's volume increases and the sea level rises even with no new water added. This accounts for roughly half of the observed rise, and it is the contribution that continues for as long as the ocean stays warm — which is why sea level keeps rising after emissions fall.
2. Melting of land ice. Glaciers and ice sheets lose mass to the ocean. Glaciers and peripheral ice caps contribute the larger share; the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets contribute less than their size suggests because so much of the melting that occurs at their margins is currently offset by increased snowfall over the interior — though that offset is shrinking.

A third, smaller term is land water storage: dams, reservoirs and groundwater extraction change how much water is stored on land.
chunks.heading: 1. Sea level rise — the mechanism, decomposed

chunks.text:
- The rates. Global mean sea level rose about 20 cm between 1901 and 2018, and the rate has accelerated: 1.3 mm per year over 1901–1971, 1.9 mm per year over 1971–2006, and 3.7 mm per year over 2006–2018. By 2025, global mean sea level stood about 111 mm above the 1993 satellite baseline — a record high for the fourteenth consecutive year.
- The key insight to write: sea level rise is not a single event but a slow ratchet that raises the baseline on which every storm surge lands, which in turn means the consequence is not bigger tides, but that the same storm surge reaches further inland and more often. A flood defence designed against the historic extreme is designed against a baseline that no longer exists.
- Local variation is large. Ocean circulation patterns, land subsidence and sedimentation all modify the local rate, so the global figure is a starting point, not a prediction for any particular coastline.
chunks.heading: 1. Sea level rise — the mechanism, decomposed

chunks.text:
- More moisture in the atmosphere. The atmosphere can hold roughly 7 per cent more water vapour per degree of warming, and evaporation from warmer oceans and land increases accordingly.
- Consequence: heavier rainfall. The same storm system delivers more rain. Global heavy precipitation increases by about 7 per cent for every 1 °C of warming. The Pakistan cloudburst of 15 August 2025, in which about 150 mm of rain fell in one hour in Buner with more than 220 deaths province-wide, is the current illustration of the mechanism.
- Consequence: more drought risk in some regions. Where warming increases evaporation more than it increases rainfall, soil moisture falls. This is the counter-intuitive point examiners like: climate change does not simply mean "more rain everywhere" — it means a redistribution, with wet areas getting wetter and dry areas getting drier in many cases.
- Consequence: more heavy rain days, fewer rain days. Hong Kong's own projection is that there is no significant trend in the total number of rain days, but the number of extreme rainfall days and the average rainfall intensity both increase. The pattern changes, not just the total.
chunks.heading: 2. Changes in the hydrological cycle

chunks.text:
- Heatwaves. The IPCC assessment is that heatwaves have become more frequent and more intense as a result of human-caused warming, and that they are among the most certain impacts. Europe in summer 2025 saw four consecutive heatwaves with at least 35,000 excess deaths, and temperatures reaching 46 °C in Germany and 45.8 °C in Spain, with over 80 million Europeans experiencing above 40 °C.
- The probability-distribution framing. Warming shifts the whole distribution of possible temperatures upward, so the threshold that defines a heatwave is crossed more often. That is why "more frequent and more intense" is the correct description and "more storms" is not.
- Cyclones. The sustained wind speed of the most intense tropical cyclones is expected to increase by roughly 1 to 2 per cent per degree of warming, and rainfall rates increase faster than that. But the total number of cyclones is expected to decrease. The exam distinction is: fewer but more intense.
- Drought and fire. Higher temperatures, lower humidity and less rainfall in some regions raise wildfire risk — the mechanism behind the 2025 European, Californian and Korean fires, and the Borneo fires.
chunks.heading: 3. Changes in temperature and extreme weather

chunks.text:
- Species migration. As the thermal envelope moves poleward and upslope, species ranges shift. Those that cannot migrate fast enough decline. This is a mechanism, not a mood: the climate moves; the species either follows or goes extinct.
- Coral bleaching. Corals expel their symbiotic algae when water exceeds their thermal tolerance, and repeated bleaching prevents recovery. The Great Barrier Reef has suffered mass bleaching events in 1998, 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022, 2024 and 2025. The biophysical limit: once the ocean is too warm often enough, the reef does not come back.
- Ocean acidification. The ocean absorbs roughly a quarter of anthropogenic CO₂, which makes surface water more acidic. Surface ocean pH has fallen by about 0.1 units since the industrial era — roughly a 26 per cent increase in hydrogen ion concentration. Shell-forming organisms need more energy to build carbonate skeletons in more acidic water, so the effect propagates up the food web.
- Sea ice and permafrost. Antarctic sea ice reached an annual minimum of about 1.98 million km² on 1 March 2025, tied for the second-lowest in the 47-year satellite record and roughly 860,000 km² below the 1981–2010 average. Arctic sea ice is declining faster than the Antarctic. Thawing permafrost releases CO₂ and methane — an impact that then feeds back.
- Glacier mass loss. In the 2025 hydrological year, glaciers lost roughly 408 ± 132 gigatonnes of mass, equivalent to about 1.1 mm of sea level rise; six of the seven highest mass-loss years on record have occurred since 2019.
chunks.heading: 4. Ecosystems and the cryosphere

chunks.text:
- Ice-albedo feedback. Less ice → darker surface → more shortwave absorbed → more warming → less ice.
- Permafrost feedback. Warming → permafrost thaw → carbon released → more warming → more thaw.
- Water vapour feedback. More warming → more moisture → more longwave trapped → more warming.

Write these as closed loops. They explain why the impacts section is also part of the causes argument, and why a candidate who can connect the two halves of the essay scores higher.
chunks.heading: 5. The two feedbacks that connect physical impacts back to causes

chunks.text:
- Describe / Explain: for each impact, give the physical process, then the consequence. Use the chain warming → process → change in a physical variable → consequence for the system.
- "Explain why sea level rise is a global problem even where the local rise differs": because the baseline rises everywhere, and the design standard of flood defences is set against the baseline.
- "Explain the relationship between sea level rise and storm surge": the surge is unchanged in height; the baseline it sits on has risen, so the same surge causes greater inundation.
- "Discuss the physical impacts for Hong Kong": hotter nights, more extreme rainfall, rising sea level, higher storm surge levels, marine heat stress on coral reefs, sea surface temperature rise.
- "Evaluate whether physical impacts matter more than social impacts": physical impacts are the cause and the social ones the expression; but the social consequences are what motivate action, and they are unevenly distributed.
chunks.heading: Answer structure

chunks.text:
- No mechanism. "Sea level rises" is the consequence; the marks are for expansion and melting.
- Saying "more storms" when the projection is fewer but more intense cyclones.
- Assuming more rain everywhere. The redistribution point — wetter wet, drier dry — is the sophisticated move.
- Missing the thermal expansion half of sea level rise.
- Confusing bleaching with death of the coral. Bleaching is the stress response; recovery is possible if conditions improve, which is why repeated bleaching is what kills reefs.
- Treating sea level rise as a step change rather than a ratchet that raises the frequency of extreme water levels.
- Attributing a specific event. Say that the likelihood and intensity changed, not that climate change "caused" that storm.
chunks.heading: Common marks lost

chunks.text:
1. Give the two main contributions to sea level rise, with their approximate shares.
2. Explain why a storm surge causes more damage in 2025 than in 1995, given the same storm.
3. Why does the atmosphere holding about 7 per cent more moisture per degree not mean "more rain everywhere"?
4. Explain the mechanism by which warming affects tropical cyclone numbers and intensity differently.
5. How does ocean acidification reach the human food chain?
6. Write the ice-albedo feedback as a closed loop.

A self-contained teaching unit built around the October 2026 Borneo / Indonesia fire event during the developing super El Niño. The data were assembled in October 2026; some figures compare the present event with the 2019 analogue and the 2020 dry-season baseline.

chunks.text:
- Thermal anomaly ≠ fire. VIIRS picks up gas flares, kilns, and sun glint too. For peat fires specifically, ESA WorldCover 2021 + peatland mask is a better proxy.
- Global Peatland Map 2.0 (Greifswald / UNEP) overestimates peat extent in Indonesia and Malaysia — that caveat is mandatory whenever you cite the country's 6 Mha peatland figure.
- Reanalysis ≠ gauge. ERA5 is a 12-point grid, not point measurements. For exam-style defensible trend claims, the GRDC daily records (free registration) are the upgrade.
- Sentinel-2 cloud cover varies. 2025 is 21% cloud, 2019 is 13% — your "more fires" comparison is on the visible ground, not a cloud-fooled change.

chunks.heading: CP7 Update Cases 2025–2026 — Global Warming

chunks.text:
- Global temperature, 2025. Mean surface temperature 1.44 °C ± 0.13 above 1850–1900; 2023–2025 the first three-year period averaging above 1.5 °C; WMO confirms 2025 as the third-warmest year on record. — WMO, 14 Jan 2026.
- Sea level, 2025. Global mean sea level ~111.2 mm above the 1993 satellite baseline — a record high for the 14th consecutive year; 2025 annual rise 0.08 cm (La Niña-suppressed) against a long-term 0.44 cm/yr trend. — AMS State of the Climate 2025; NASA Sea Level Portal.
- Glacier loss, 2025 hydrological year. Glaciers lost 408 ± 132 Gt of mass — equivalent to 1.1 mm of sea-level rise; six of the seven highest mass-loss years have occurred since 2019. — Nature Reviews Earth & Environment / WGMS (Welty et al., 2026).
- Antarctic sea ice, 1 Mar 2025. Annual minimum 1.98 million km² — tied for second-lowest in the 47-year record, 860,000 km² below the 1981–2010 average; fourth straight minimum under 2 million km². — NSIDC, 6 Mar 2025.

chunks.text:
- Europe, summer 2025 heatwaves. At least 35,000 excess deaths across four back-to-back heatwaves; 46 °C in Germany (28 June), 45.8 °C in Spain; over 80 million Europeans experienced above 40 °C. — The Guardian, 25 Aug 2026; BBC.
- Pakistan, 15 Aug 2025. Buner cloudburst dropped ~150 mm of rain in one hour; at least 222 killed province-wide (208 in Buner); 2025 monsoon total about 1,000 deaths. — AFP; Dawn, 16 Aug 2025.

chunks.heading: 2.1 Distribution

chunks.text:
Granite (5 steps):
1. Magma generated
2. Magma rises but stops underground
3. Slow cooling → large crystals
4. Solidifies
5. Uplift → exposed

Tuff (5 steps):
1. Volcanic eruption
2. Ash ejected into air
3. Ash settles
4. Compaction → tuff
5. Uplift → exposed

chunks.heading: 2.2 Sedimentary Rocks

chunks.text:
1. Weathering & erosion break existing rock into sediment (sand, mud, pebbles).
2. Transportation carries it (river, wind, sea).
3. Deposition — sediment settles in layers when the water slows; each layer is laid down horizontally (original horizontality).
4. Compaction — burial under later layers: weight squeezes water out, grains pack tighter.
5. Cementation — minerals (silica, calcite, iron oxides) precipitate in the pore spaces and glue grains together.
6. The two last steps together = lithification — sediment becomes rock.
chunks.heading: How sedimentary rock forms (the chain, in order)

chunks.text:
| Feature | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| Bedding plane | Surface between two layers — marks a change in deposition conditions (grain size, material) |
| Stratification | The layering itself; layers may be folded or faulted by later internal forces (compression) |
| Fossils | Organic remains preserved between layers — a sedimentary signature (igneous rocks have none) |
| Grain size | Conglomerate (pebbles) → sandstone (sand) → mudstone (mud); finer = quieter deposition |
chunks.heading: Key features you must be able to use

chunks.text:
- Layered sedimentary rocks occur mainly in the northeast (Tolo Harbour / Sha Lo Tung area — Devonian sandstone & mudstone, over 300 million years old).
- Recent alluvium (unconsolidated sediment) fills the northwestern New Territories lowlands.
- Contrast for identification: HK granite = coarse-grained, massive (no bedding), well-jointed; sedimentary = visible layers + bedding planes.
chunks.heading: Hong Kong context

chunks.text:
- Sedimentary rock origin: deposition in layers → burial → compaction → cementation → bedding planes separate the layers.
- Why weaker than granite: often bedded and porous — water enters along bedding planes/joints → breaks down faster (links 4.1 Weathering).
chunks.heading: Exam chains

chunks.text:
1. A rock shows clear layers and a fossil. Name the rock type and the process that bound its grains. → Sedimentary; cementation (with compaction).
2. What forms a bedding plane? → A surface between two layers, formed when deposition conditions change.
3. Layers in the rock are bent into a curve — external or internal process? → Internal (compression/deformation after the rock formed).
